META.subject: Physics
META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 3.4 (9 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Physics
UNIT.content:
• Electric charges: positive and negative charges, charge on atoms and subatomic particles
• Charging by friction: transfer of electrons between insulators (rubbed balloon, polythene, perspex, ebonite, glass, silk, fur)
• Conductors and insulators: free electrons, bound electrons, examples in Kenyan homes and industry
• Charging by contact and by induction: using an electroscope, earthing
• Law of electrostatics: like charges repel, unlike charges attract; charging and attraction of neutral objects
• Distribution of charge on conductors: charge on the outer surface, effect of shape, action of points (corona discharge)
• Detecting and measuring charge: the gold-leaf electroscope, charge detection, testing the sign of charge, discharging
• Applications of electrostatics: lightning conductors, photocopiers, electrostatic precipitators in cement factories, paint spraying, crop spraying
• Hazards of static electricity and safety: lightning, fuel tanker earthing, static in dry environments
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) Describe the origin of electric charges and how materials become charged
b) Distinguish between conductors and insulators of electricity
c) Investigate charging of conductors by contact and induction
d) Explain the distribution of charge on a conductor
e) Detect and measure electric charge using a gold-leaf electroscope
f) Appreciate the application of electrostatics in everyday life
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Critical thinking and problem solving: learners analyse evidence from charging activities to explain attractions and repulsions and to predict outcomes in new situations
• Communication and collaboration: learners work in groups to carry out investigations, share observations, and defend explanations using evidence
• Creativity and imagination: learners design simple electroscopes and devices from locally available materials
• Digital literacy: learners use simulations to visualise the movement of electrons during charging
• Learning to learn: learners revisit the Driving Question Board and revise their models as understanding grows
UNIT.values:
• Responsibility: learners handle electrical materials and equipment safely and care for shared apparatus
• Integrity: learners report observations honestly even when results differ from predictions
• Unity: learners cooperate in groups to carry out investigations and build shared models
• Respect: learners listen to and value the ideas of others during discussions
UNIT.sep:
• Asking questions and defining problems: learners generate questions about the balloon, hair and paper on the Driving Question Board
• Developing and using models: learners build and revise a particle model of electron transfer
• Planning and carrying out investigations: learners test materials for charging and conduction
• Analysing and interpreting data: learners interpret electroscope observations
• Constructing explanations: learners explain attraction of neutral objects using charge ideas
• Engaging in argument from evidence: learners debate explanations of charge distribution
UNIT.pcis:
• Safety and security: learners learn lightning safety and the safe handling of fuel and electrical equipment
• Environmental education: electrostatic precipitators reduce dust pollution from cement factories
• Life skills: learners apply decision making when protecting themselves and property from lightning
• Education for sustainable development: learners relate electrostatic technologies to efficient use of resources, such as crop spraying
UNIT.careers:
• Electrical engineer: designs safe electrical systems and lightning protection for buildings in Nairobi and Mombasa
• Electronics technician: handles static-sensitive components when repairing phones and computers
• Meteorologist: studies lightning and thunderstorms, such as those in the Lake Victoria basin
• Industrial or chemical engineer: applies electrostatic precipitators and spray painting in factories
• Agricultural technologist: uses electrostatic crop sprayers on farms in Kericho and the Rift Valley
• Photocopier technician: services machines that rely on electrostatic charge
UNIT.focus: This unit uses the puzzling behaviour of a rubbed balloon to drive learners to investigate where electric charges come from and how they behave. Learners predict, observe, explain, record questions on the Driving Question Board, and progressively revise a particle model of charge across nine lessons. The unit connects to Kenyan contexts such as lightning in Kisumu, cement dust control and fuel tanker safety.
UNIT.phenomenon: When you rub a balloon on your hair, your hair stands up and follows the balloon as you pull it away. The same balloon then sticks to a classroom wall for several minutes without glue or tape, and small pieces of paper jump toward it without touching it. On a dry day in Nairobi, a learner may also feel a small shock after combing hair or removing a woollen jersey. It is puzzling because nothing visible connects the balloon to the hair, wall or paper, and the balloon was never magnetic or plugged into electricity. What causes these mysterious forces? Where do the charges come from? Why does the balloon sometimes attract and sometimes repel? Students observe these surprising attractions and repulsions and wonder about the invisible forces at work.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A plastic comb rubbed on dry hair picks up tiny pieces of paper or sukuma wiki leaf fragments
• Lightning flashes during thunderstorms over Kisumu and Lake Victoria, and tall buildings are fitted with lightning conductors
• Fuel tankers delivering petrol in Mombasa trail an earthing chain to prevent sparks
• Cement factories use electrostatic precipitators so that chimneys release less dust
• A gold-leaf electroscope leaf rises when a charged rod is brought near the cap, without touching it
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects?
2. What are electric charges?
3. Why do some materials conduct electricity while others don’t?
4. How can we charge conductors?
5. Where does charge go on a conductor?
6. How can we detect and measure electric charge?
7. How is electrostatics used in everyday life?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Anchoring phenomenon. Students rub balloons on hair, stick them to walls and lift paper pieces; they record observations and questions on the Driving Question Board and draw initial models.
Lesson 2: What are electric charges? Students study atoms, protons, electrons and neutrons, and test the rule that like charges repel and unlike charges attract using rubbed rods and strips.
Lesson 3: Charging by friction. Students rub different materials (polythene, perspex, ebonite, glass, silk, fur), identify the sign of charge, and model electron transfer to explain the balloon and hair.
Lesson 4: Conductors and insulators. Students test materials such as copper, aluminium, plastic, wood and metal spoons, and explain differences using free electrons.
Lesson 5: Charging by contact. Students charge conductors by touching with a charged rod, and explain the sign of charge gained using electron movement.
Lesson 6: Charging by induction and earthing. Students charge conductors without touching them and explain how this clarifies why neutral paper is attracted to the balloon.
Lesson 7: Distribution of charge on conductors. Students investigate charge on outer surfaces and at points, and explain sparks and lightning conductors.
Lesson 8: Detecting and measuring charge. Students use a gold-leaf electroscope to detect charge, find its sign and discharge it, and relate leaf divergence to amount of charge.
Lesson 9: Applications and consolidation. Students analyse applications such as lightning conductors, photocopiers, electrostatic precipitators and fuel tanker earthing, revise their final model, and answer the main driving question using the Driving Question Board.

LESSONS.title: The Mysterious Balloon: What Invisible Force Is at Work?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: electrostatic force, attraction, repulsion, electric charge, Driving Question Board, humidity, model

slo.purpose: To launch the anchoring phenomenon of the mysterious balloon, so that learners observe and describe electrostatic attraction and repulsion without explaining it, record their questions on the Driving Question Board (DQB), and draw initial models that will be revised in every later lesson.
slo.knowledge: Learners describe what a rubbed balloon does to hair, a wall and paper pieces, and what an unrubbed balloon does. They distinguish attraction from repulsion, and note that the effect is weaker on humid days (Mombasa, about 80%) than on dry days (Nairobi, about 35%).
slo.skills: Predicting, observing and recording carefully, asking testable questions (NGSS SEP 1: Asking Questions), developing and using models (NGSS SEP 2), planning a fair comparison with a control (unrubbed balloon), and communicating observations in talk and sketches.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about invisible forces, willingness to say 'I do not know yet', respect for classmates' ideas, safe and careful handling of materials, and honesty in recording what is actually seen rather than what is expected.
slo.keyInquiry: Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the opening lesson. It creates a shared experience and a need to know. Learners use only prior knowledge of magnets and everyday experiences such as combing hair. Explanations are deliberately withheld. Their questions populate the DQB, which drives Lessons 2 to 9, and their initial models are revised after every lesson.
slo.safetyNotes: Use only dry, inflated latex balloons and check for latex allergy beforehand (use a polythene bag or another material for affected learners). Balloons must not be put in the mouth. Burst balloons are picked up at once to avoid choking. Keep thread lengths short. Handle scissors carefully when tearing or cutting paper. Rubbing is done gently, and no one pulls another learner's hair. Teacher demonstrations are done in dry conditions.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Mwangi opens by asking learners about a time they felt a small shock or saw hair stand up after combing on a dry Nairobi morning. Learners predict what a balloon rubbed on hair will do, then work in groups of four to observe the phenomenon: 20 strokes of the balloon on dry hair, hair rising and following the balloon up to about 5 cm, the balloon sticking to the painted wall for about 3 minutes, torn paper pieces (about 1 cm x 1 cm) jumping up when the balloon is held about 2 cm above them, and two rubbed balloons on threads pushing apart. An unrubbed balloon serves as the control and does nothing. Learners then compare what they saw with Amina's report from Mombasa (humid, about 80%, it hardly works) and consider the Nairobi dry-day figure (about 35%). They describe the patterns with words such as attract and repel but do not explain them. Learners compare the effect with what they know about magnets, build the Driving Question Board (DQB) from their own questions, and draw initial particle-level or cause-and-effect models of the balloon, hair, wall and paper. These are kept for revision in later lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall everyday experiences: Wanjiru notices her hair stands up after combing on dry mornings in Nairobi, and others describe the small shock from a woollen jersey. Mr Mwangi shows a latex balloon. Individually, learners write and sketch predictions in their notebooks: (1) What will happen to my hair if I rub the balloon on it 20 times and pull it away slowly? (2) What will happen if I put the rubbed balloon against the wall? (3) What will happen if I hold it about 2 cm above small pieces of paper? (4) Will an unrubbed balloon do the same? They compare with a partner and then share with the group. They also state whether the balloon is like a magnet and give a reason.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Think about the last time you combed your hair on a dry morning. What did you notice? Turn to your partner and tell them.' Allow 1 minute for talk, then take WAIT TIME of 10 seconds before calling on anyone. Cold-call 3 learners, including Wanjiru, for their experiences. Hold up the balloon and say: 'I am not going to tell you what happens. I want your best prediction, and I want to hear your reasoning, not just your answer.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10 seconds before asking: 'Who predicts the balloon will behave like a magnet? Who disagrees? What makes you say that?' Cold-call 4 more learners to share and record predictions on the board in a tally. Do NOT confirm or correct any prediction. Say: 'All ideas are welcome today. We will test them.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-and-Reason (Think-Pair-Share): writing a prediction and a reason before seeing anything commits learners to an idea, so the later surprise becomes a real conflict between expectation and evidence. It also surfaces prior knowledge of magnets and combing hair that the teacher can build on in later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that at least 80% of learners wrote a prediction for all four questions plus a reason. Look for ideas such as 'it is magnetic', 'the hair is sticky', 'static' or 'nothing will happen'. Note which learners refer to magnets and which refer to everyday experiences. Record in the tally how many predict attraction, repulsion or no effect. Do not grade for correctness.

framework.learnerExperience: Station 1, Hair: Each group of four rubs a dry balloon on the hair of one willing member for 20 strokes (about 10 seconds), then slowly pulls it away. They record what the hair does and the greatest distance (about 5 cm) at which hair strands follow the balloon. Station 2, Wall: They press the rubbed balloon against the painted wall, let go, and time how long it stays (about 3 minutes, range 2 to 5 minutes). Station 3, Paper: They tear paper into pieces of about 1 cm x 1 cm on a desk, hold the rubbed balloon about 2 cm above them, and record what happens, including pieces that jump up and then fall off again after touching the balloon. Station 4, Two balloons: They rub two balloons on hair, hang them from separate threads, bring them near each other, and record that they push apart. Control: An unrubbed balloon is tried on hair, wall and paper: no effect. They record all results in an observation table with columns 'What I did', 'What I saw', 'Attract / Repel / No effect'. Mr Mwangi then shows data: on a humid day in Mombasa (about 80% relative humidity) the balloon sticks for under 30 seconds or not at all, and in Nairobi's dry season (about 35%) a small shock is felt after removing a woollen jersey, with a faint crackle heard in a dark room.
framework.teacherMoves: Before starting say: 'Your job right now is to be a careful observer. Write what you SEE, not why you think it happens.' Circulate and ask each group: 'What exactly did the hair do? How far from the balloon was it still moving?' and 'What did the unrubbed balloon do, and why do we test it?' If a group says 'because of static', respond: 'Static is a name. Tell me what you actually saw.' Remind all groups to use dry conditions and pick up burst balloons. After 20 minutes, stop and say: 'Hands down, pencils down. Look at your table.' WAIT TIME of 10 seconds. Cold-call 4 groups to report one observation each: hair, wall, paper, two balloons. Ask Otieno to describe the sticking balloon. Then show or read the humid-day data and say: 'Amina says it never works at her coastal home in the rainy season. What does our table tell us about conditions?' WAIT TIME of 15 seconds before taking responses from 3 learners. Ask Kipchoge to share his question about whether the shock is like lightning, and write it down for the DQB without answering it.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Observation with a Control (NGSS SEP 3: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations): separating 'what I did', 'what I saw' and 'attract/repel/no effect' lets learners describe patterns without explaining them. The unrubbed balloon shows that rubbing is the cause of the effects, and the Nairobi and Mombasa data show that conditions matter, so learners see that the effect is real, repeatable and dependent on conditions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether tables contain measurable details: about 5 cm for hair, about 3 minutes for the wall, about 2 cm for paper, balloons pushing apart, and no effect from the unrubbed balloon. Indicators of success: learners write what they saw without explanations, use the words attract and repel correctly, and record the control result. Note groups that report that paper pieces fall off after touching the balloon, which is a detail to return to in Lesson 5. Ask each learner to state one difference between dry and humid days using the data.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in the same groups to sort their observations into two categories on a chart: 'Things that came together (attract)' and 'Things that moved apart (repel)'. They note which observations do not fit easily into either, such as the paper pieces that jump up and then fall off. Each group writes a 'we notice' statement (for example, 'The rubbed balloon pulls on hair, wall and paper without touching them, but the unrubbed balloon does not') and a 'we wonder' statement. They then compare the balloon with a magnet from prior knowledge, listing what is the same (pulls without touching) and what is different (does not need a metal object, pushes balloons apart, effect fades, depends on rubbing and weather). They share ideas about what could be happening but are told to treat them as hunches that will be tested, not final answers.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'We are not explaining yet. We are describing patterns. Which things came together? Which moved apart? What do you notice?' Give 8 minutes for group sorting. Circulate and ask: 'How do you know the balloon pulled the paper and the paper did not just move by itself?' (the unrubbed balloon control). Then ask: 'Is this a magnet? Think about the wall and the paper. What is the same and what is different?' WAIT TIME of 15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners, one at a time, and ask each to build on the previous answer: 'Do you agree, and what would you add?' Record 'notice' statements on the board. If a learner proposes an explanation (for instance, 'tiny charges'), say: 'That is an interesting hunch. Write it on a sticky note for our DQB and we will test it over the coming lessons.' Do NOT confirm. Close with: 'What is the one thing we are all sure about, based on evidence?' Take 2 responses.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Notice-and-Wonder with Pattern Sorting (Constructing Explanations, NGSS SEP 6): sorting observations into attract and repel separates evidence from interpretation and builds a shared vocabulary. Comparing with magnets uses prior knowledge, then shows its limits, which creates productive uncertainty rather than an early, shallow answer.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each group's chart separates observations from ideas and includes at least three entries in each category. Listen for correct use of 'attract' and 'repel' and for statements supported by evidence, such as the control. Success indicator: at least 3 groups identify at least one difference between the balloon and a magnet. Note any learners who say a balloon is 'magnetic' for later follow-up in Lesson 2. Collect the 'we wonder' statements as raw material for the DQB.

framework.learnerExperience: The class builds its first Driving Question Board on a chart or wall space. The central question is written at the top: 'Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects?' Each learner writes at least two questions on separate sticky notes, such as 'What is the invisible thing the balloon gives to my hair?', 'Why does the balloon stick longer in Nairobi than in Mombasa?', 'Is the shock from my jersey like lightning?' (Kipchoge), 'Why does my hair stand up on dry mornings?' (Wanjiru) and 'Why do two balloons push apart?'. In groups they cluster similar questions and give each cluster a heading, for example 'What is it?', 'Why does weather matter?', 'Why attract and why repel?', 'Is this lightning?', 'Where is it used?'. They place the clusters on the board and may add the KICD inquiry questions as the teacher reads them aloud. They agree which questions they hope to answer first.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Good scientists keep track of what they wonder. Write at least two questions, one about what you saw and one about why it might happen.' Model a good question: 'Why does the balloon stick longer on some days?' and a weaker question: 'Is it good?'. Give 5 minutes for writing. WAIT TIME of 10 seconds before asking: 'Who will share a question that puzzles you most?' Cold-call 5 learners, including Amina, Wanjiru and Kipchoge, and place their notes on the board. Then ask groups to cluster the questions, giving 6 minutes. Walk around asking: 'What is the common idea in these questions?' Read aloud the seven KICD inquiry questions and ask: 'Which of your clusters match these?' Say: 'We will return to this board at the end of every lesson, moving questions we can answer and adding new ones.' Take a photo or label the board so it can be reused.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (Asking Questions, NGSS SEP 1): learner-generated questions give ownership of the learning and make the unit storyline visible. Clustering shows the links between questions and helps learners see that one big phenomenon needs several investigations, so each later lesson has a clear purpose.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that every learner contributed at least two questions and that at least 70% are about cause or mechanism (why or how) rather than yes/no. Look for questions that link to weather (Amina), shocks and lightning (Kipchoge) and hair (Wanjiru). Success indicator: groups can explain the heading of their cluster in one sentence. Note common clusters to match them to Lessons 2 to 9.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner draws an Initial Model on a sheet of paper (to be kept in a folder) showing the balloon, the hair, the wall and a paper piece before and after rubbing. They use arrows and labels to show what they think is happening, including anything they think moves, is made or is passed on, even if they cannot name it yet. They add a short caption: 'I think the balloon attracts the hair because ...'. A key box lists symbols they have used. In groups they compare their models, mark one similarity and one difference with a coloured pencil, and write one 'I am not sure about ...' statement. They finish by completing the Summary Table (What we observed / What we learned / How we can explain it so far).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A model is a drawing that shows what you think is happening, including things we cannot see. There are no wrong models today. They are your starting point.' Show an example of a blank layout with four boxes (balloon, hair, wall, paper) but do not draw any particles. Give 10 minutes of silent drawing. Circulate and ask: 'What does your arrow show? Is something moving? What do you think is moving?' Do not correct. Then give 5 minutes for group comparison. WAIT TIME of 10 seconds before asking: 'What did someone else draw that you had not thought of?' Cold-call 4 learners. Say: 'Keep your model safe. In the next lesson we look inside materials to see what we are made of, and you will revise it.' Close by returning to the DQB: 'Which question do you most hope we answer next?' Take 3 responses.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial Model Drawing (Developing and Using Models, NGSS SEP 2): putting ideas on paper before instruction exposes learners' current thinking and gives a baseline that can be revised in each lesson. Comparing models highlights different ideas, which produces genuine questions and shows the value of evidence in changing a model.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each model includes all four objects (balloon, hair, wall, paper) and some form of cause (arrow, symbol or word) for attraction. Success indicators: at least 60% of learners label something invisible as moving or acting, and each learner writes one uncertainty statement. Note misconceptions such as 'the balloon is magnetic', 'the air pushes the paper' or 'glue-like stickiness' for targeted work in Lessons 2 and 3. Review Summary Tables for observations that are written as observations, not explanations.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learner predictions and initial models revealed ideas about magnets, air or stickiness that need to be revisited in Lesson 2? Did all groups keep observation and explanation separate, and did they use the unrubbed balloon as a control? How many DQB questions were about cause rather than description? Did the dry-versus-humid contrast (Nairobi about 35%, Mombasa about 80%) prompt strong questions, and did Amina and Kipchoge feel their contributions were valued? What conditions (dry rooms, allergy-safe materials, balloon supply) need to be adjusted for the next lesson?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: After 20 strokes on dry hair, the rubbed balloon made hair strands rise and follow it up to about 5 cm, stuck to the wall for about 3 minutes, and made 1 cm x 1 cm paper pieces jump up when held about 2 cm above them, with some falling off again. Two rubbed balloons on threads pushed apart. An unrubbed balloon did nothing. The effect is weak or absent on humid days (Mombasa, about 80%) and strong on dry days (Nairobi, about 35%).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Rubbing makes the balloon able to pull on hair, wall and paper without touching them, and to push away another rubbed balloon. The effect is not the same as a magnet, it fades with time and it depends on the weather. We now have many questions on our DQB.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: So far we can only describe what happens: something invisible passes between the rubbed balloon and other objects, and rubbing and dry air seem to matter. Our initial models are hunches, and we do not yet know where the effect comes from or why the balloon sometimes attracts and sometimes repels.

LESSONS.title: What Are Electric Charges? Atoms, Protons, Electrons and the Rule of Attraction and Repulsion
LESSONS.aresKeywords: electric charge, coulomb, atom, proton, electron, neutron, neutral atom, nucleus, like charges repel, unlike charges attract, electrostatic force, polythene strip, perspex rod

slo.purpose: To help learners explain what electric charges are by describing the atom (protons +, electrons -, neutrons 0), showing why neutral atoms have no overall charge, and testing with rubbed rods and strips the rule that like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
slo.knowledge: Learners describe an atom as a nucleus of protons (+1.6 x 10^-19 C) and neutrons (0 C) surrounded by electrons (-1.6 x 10^-19 C). A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. Electric charge has symbol Q and unit coulomb (C). Like charges repel and unlike charges attract; this force is called the electrostatic force.
slo.skills: Making predictions from a rule; carrying out a simple investigation with rods and strips; recording and tabulating observations; using evidence to develop and revise a particle-level model (NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models; Planning and Carrying Out Investigations; Constructing Explanations).
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about invisible particles; honesty in recording results even when they differ from predictions; cooperation when sharing apparatus; appreciation that scientists use evidence to infer what cannot be seen.
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 left us with the observations that two rubbed balloons push apart and a rubbed balloon and hair pull together, and with many questions on the DQB. In this lesson learners find out what electric charge is and test the rule that like charges repel and unlike charges attract. This gives them the particle vocabulary (protons, electrons, neutrons) needed in Lesson 3, where they ask how rubbing gives the balloon and hair their charges.
slo.safetyNotes: Use only light polythene strips and perspex rods; keep them away from faces. Teachers keep all materials dry (humidity makes the activity fail). Handle threads and stands carefully so rods do not fall. Do not use mains electricity. Keep the floor clear of dropped threads and paper pieces. Wash hands after handling cloths and materials.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by recalling the Lesson 1 observation that two rubbed balloons on threads pushed apart while a rubbed balloon and hair pulled together, and predict what will happen with other rubbed objects. They then gather evidence in two ways: (1) a rods-and-strips investigation (polythene strip rubbed with wool/fur, perspex rod rubbed with silk) to test attraction and repulsion between pairs, and (2) a reading and card-sorting activity on the atom with charge values of the proton, electron and neutron. In the Explain phase they use both sets of evidence to answer: what are electric charges, why is a normal atom neutral, and what is the rule about like and unlike charges? Learners add questions to the DQB and draw a first particle-level model of the balloon, hair, wall and paper showing only what Lesson 2 supports: that matter contains positive and negative charges and that charges of the same sign repel while opposite signs attract. How the balloon and hair get their charges is left to Lesson 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the Lesson 1 observation: two balloons, each rubbed on hair and hung on separate threads, pushed apart, while a rubbed balloon and hair pulled together. Individually they write for 3 minutes: 'If I rub a polythene strip with wool/fur and hang it on a thread, and bring a second identical rubbed strip near it, what will happen? What if I bring a rubbed perspex rod instead?' They write a prediction and a reason in their notebooks (a 'forces between charged objects' prediction table with three pairs: polythene-polythene, perspex-perspex, polythene-perspex). Learners also write one idea about what is inside a 'tiny piece' of balloon rubber that could make it push or pull.
framework.teacherMoves: Mr Mwangi displays the sentence from Lesson 1: 'Two rubbed balloons pushed apart; a rubbed balloon and hair pulled together.' Ask: "Last lesson we saw pushing and pulling with nothing touching. What do you think is inside the balloon and hair that could cause this?" Give 3 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before calling on anyone. Cold-call 4 learners (e.g. Otieno, Wanjiru, plus two others) to share predictions; ask each, "What makes you think that?" Do NOT confirm or correct. Record predictions for the three pairs on the board as tally marks (attract / repel / nothing). Ask Kipchoge's earlier question: "Is there a 'pushing' type and a 'pulling' type of invisible thing?" and leave it open.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with reasoning (Predict-Observe-Explain). Learners commit to a prediction and a reason before seeing data, which makes their current ideas visible and creates a 'need to know'. Linking to the Lesson 1 balloon observations connects the new investigation to the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check notebooks: (1) learners have written a prediction for all three pairs; (2) at least one reason is given for each; (3) listen for ideas such as 'same things push, different things pull' or 'something tiny inside' versus 'magnetism'. Tally the class predictions and note the proportion expecting polythene-polythene to repel. Note learners who attribute the force to magnetism or electricity from a plug; these are targets for the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (about 25 minutes), groups of 4 with Mr Mwangi's dry materials: two polythene strips, two perspex rods, a wool/fur cloth, a silk cloth, thread and a stand or clamp. 1. Rub one polythene strip with wool/fur (20 strokes) and hang it from a thread. Rub a second polythene strip the same way and bring it near without touching. Record: attract, repel or no effect. 2. Repeat with two perspex rods each rubbed with silk (20 strokes). 3. Bring a silk-rubbed perspex rod near the hanging polythene strip. 4. As a control, bring an unrubbed polythene strip and an unrubbed perspex rod near the hanging strip. Learners fill the table: two polythene strips repel; two perspex rods repel; polythene and perspex attract; unrubbed objects show no effect. They note that the polythene strip rubbed with wool/fur is called negative and the perspex rod rubbed with silk is called positive (the teacher gives these labels; the reason is for Lesson 3). Part B (about 15 minutes): learners read the 'Inside the Atom' card set and complete the charge table: proton +1.6 x 10^-19 C, electron -1.6 x 10^-19 C, neutron 0 C. They sort cards to build a neutral atom (for example 3 protons, 4 neutrons, 3 electrons) and a second atom with 3 protons and 2 electrons, and calculate the total charge of each: 0 C for the first atom; +1.6 x 10^-19 C for the second.
framework.teacherMoves: Demonstrate hanging a strip and bringing the second near it, without giving results. Say: "Keep the strokes the same, 20 each, and keep everything dry so the effect shows clearly." Circulate with the prompt: "What exactly did the strip do when the second one came close? Describe it, do not explain it yet." Ask a group that gets no effect: "What could be affecting the rubbing or the dryness?" (Amina's humidity point from Lesson 1: damp materials let charge escape.) For Part B ask: "Which particle has no charge? How do you know from the table?" Wait 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 3 groups to report their table results; ask others to show thumbs up if their results match. Chart the class results on the board. If a group's results conflict, repeat the trial publicly. Do not use the phrase 'static electricity' as an explanation; use 'electric charge' and 'electrostatic force'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table and pattern-finding. Collecting the same measurements across groups lets learners see consistent patterns (same objects repel, different objects attract) rather than isolated events. The atom card sort gives a particle-level resource that makes charge a property of matter, preparing learners to use the pattern in the Explain phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners fill in all rows of the rods-and-strips table including the unrubbed controls; (2) learners use the words attract and repel accurately; (3) the atom card sort shows 3 protons and 3 electrons for the neutral atom and learners calculate total charge 0 C; (4) learners can say the proton and electron charges have equal size (1.6 x 10^-19 C) but opposite signs. Look for learners who think neutrons have charge or that the neutral atom has no charges inside at all.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 learners prepare a 'claim-evidence-reasoning' response to three questions on a poster: (1) What are electric charges and what carries them in an atom? (2) Why is a normal atom neutral if it contains charged particles? (3) What rule do the rods-and-strips results support, and how does it explain Lesson 1's two balloons pushing apart and balloon-hair pulling together? Learners use their tables: two polythene strips repel and two perspex rods repel (like charges repel); polythene and perspex attract (unlike charges attract). They write the rule 'Like charges repel, unlike charges attract' and state that the force is the electrostatic force. They apply it: two rubbed balloons both carry the same type of charge so they repel; a balloon and hair attract, so they carry opposite types. They compare their Predict-phase ideas with the evidence and write one sentence beginning 'I used to think ... now I think ...'. Learners also answer: 'A neutral atom has 6 protons; how many electrons does it have, and what is the total charge?' (6 electrons; 0 C). Finally they note the unanswered issue: the particles that make charge are inside every atom, so why do ordinary objects not push or pull each other all the time? This is added to the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Use evidence from our table, not just what you remember, to back up each claim." Give 5 minutes of silent individual planning, then 8 minutes in groups. Then run a gallery walk: each group posts a poster and 2 learners stay to explain while others rotate. After rotation, ask: "Which pair of results tells us that like charges repel?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Ask: "Why do the balloons in Lesson 1 push apart if both were rubbed on hair?" Cold-call 2 more learners and probe: "What does that tell you about the charge on each balloon?" Press on the neutral atom: "If protons are positive and electrons are negative, why does an ordinary piece of rubber not attract everything?" Guide learners to equal numbers of protons and electrons. Correct, in Kenyan terms, the idea that charge is 'made': say "Charges are already in the atoms of the balloon, hair and cloth." Do not yet explain how rubbing separates them (Lesson 3) or why neutral paper is attracted (Lesson 6). Record: 'Where does the unlike charge on the hair come from?' as a question for Lesson 3.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with gallery walk. Learners must connect each claim to specific rows in their data, which builds scientific argumentation. Peer explanation at the posters exposes gaps and lets learners refine their reasoning. Applying the rule back to the two balloons and balloon-hair observations from Lesson 1 ties the abstract atom idea to the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) posters state that protons are positive, electrons negative, neutrons uncharged, with the correct values; (2) the neutral-atom explanation mentions equal numbers of protons and electrons so charges cancel; (3) the rule is stated with matching evidence (polythene-polythene repel etc.); (4) learners apply the rule to the two-balloon observation. Use a 3-question exit check: 'What is the charge of an atom with 8 protons and 8 electrons?', 'Do two negative strips attract or repel?', 'What is the charge of a neutron?' Aim for 80% correct. Note learners who say a neutral atom has no charges at all, or who say unlike charges repel.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB from Lesson 1. In pairs they write new questions on sticky notes that came from today's evidence, such as 'What makes the polythene strip negative after rubbing?', 'Why did only electrons and not protons matter?', 'Why does the balloon also stick to a neutral wall if neutral atoms have no overall charge?', 'Is the charge on the balloon the same size as the charge on one electron?', 'Is the shock Kipchoge felt from a jersey like lightning?'. They place notes under the key question 'What are electric charges?' and move any Lesson 1 note that is now partly answered (for example 'why do two balloons push apart?') to a 'partly answered' section with a short evidence label such as 'like charges repel (rods and strips table)'. They add one 'we now know' card: 'Atoms contain + protons, - electrons and neutral neutrons; like charges repel and unlike charges attract.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at the board from Lesson 1. Which questions can we now partly answer, and what new ones has today's evidence raised?" Give 3 minutes for pairs to write questions, then WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before sharing. Cold-call 4 pairs to read and place a question; ask: "What evidence from today helps with this, or what do we still need?" Cluster questions by theme (how charge is gained, how charge moves, neutral objects attracted, shocks and lightning). Highlight Wanjiru's question about her hair after combing and point to the 'how are charges gained?' cluster for Lesson 3. Do not answer the new questions; say: "We will return to these as we collect more evidence."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a class record of knowledge and gaps. Learners see how evidence answers part of the driving question and how each answer produces new questions, creating a sense of purposeful progress across lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe: (1) at least one new question per pair that links to today's evidence; (2) questions go beyond description (for example 'why' and 'how' questions); (3) learners can name the evidence that partly answers a moved question; (4) learners recognise which new questions need later lessons. Note pairs with only recall questions and prompt them with 'What could you ask about how the strip became charged?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise their Lesson 1 initial model, a labelled particle-level diagram of the balloon, hair, wall and paper. In their notebooks they draw a zoomed-in view of a small patch of balloon rubber and a hair strand, showing atoms as circles with a central nucleus labelled 'protons (+) and neutrons (0)' and electrons (-) around it, with equal numbers of + and - so each atom is neutral. They then add arrows and labels for the Lesson 1 observations they can now support: two balloons pushing apart (like charges repel, arrow labelled 'electrostatic force') and balloon and hair pulling together (unlike charges attract). They mark balloon with '?' for 'how did it get its charge?' and write 'Model revision 2: what changed and why?' listing evidence (rods and strips table; charge values of proton +1.6 x 10^-19 C, electron -1.6 x 10^-19 C, neutron 0 C). They add a key and a note of what the model cannot yet explain: how the balloon and hair got their charges, why neutral paper and wall are attracted.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Your model must show what we have evidence for today, and mark with a question mark what we do not know yet." Show a quick exemplar with an atom and legend on the board but leave the balloon and hair incomplete. Give 10 minutes of silent drawing, then 5 minutes of pair sharing. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before asking: "What did you add or change from your first model, and what evidence made you do that?" Cold-call 3 learners to explain their change. Prompt: "Does your model show any particle moving yet?" (not yet; that is Lesson 3). Remind learners to keep their model for Lesson 3. Collect notebooks for quick review.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Iterative model revision. Learners return to their original model, add the evidence-based ideas from this lesson and mark uncertainties. This makes the growth in understanding visible and models how scientists refine explanations as new evidence appears.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) atoms drawn with protons and neutrons in the nucleus and electrons outside; (2) equal numbers of + and - in neutral atoms; (3) arrows or labels for repulsion between like charges and attraction between unlike charges; (4) the model avoids claiming charge moves or is created; (5) a short 'what changed and why' statement referring to evidence. Common gaps: placing electrons in the nucleus, or showing unequal numbers of + and - in neutral objects.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson reflect: Did most learners get consistent repel/attract results in the rods-and-strips activity? If some groups saw no effect, was dryness or rubbing the cause (Amina's humidity point)? Could learners use the words proton, electron and neutron correctly and say why a neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons? Did any learners think charge is created or that positive charge moves in solids? (Note these for Lesson 3, where electron transfer is introduced.) Which DQB questions show curiosity about how the balloon and hair got their charges? Did learners rely on evidence from the table rather than memory in their claims? What would you change in pacing for the Observe phase?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Two polythene strips rubbed with wool/fur repel; two perspex rods rubbed with silk repel; a polythene strip and a perspex rod attract; unrubbed strips and rods do nothing. Proton charge is +1.6 x 10^-19 C, electron charge is -1.6 x 10^-19 C and neutron charge is 0 C.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Atoms contain positive protons and neutral neutrons in the nucleus with negative electrons around it. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so the total charge is 0 C. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract through the electrostatic force.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The two rubbed balloons in Lesson 1 pushed apart because they carry the same type of charge, while the balloon and hair attracted because they carry opposite types. We still need to find out how rubbing gives objects their charge and why neutral objects such as paper and the wall are also attracted.

reading.title: Electric Charge and Electric Force Practice

LESSONS.title: Charging by Friction: Who Wins the Electrons?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: charging by friction, electron transfer, triboelectric order, conservation of charge, repulsion test, electric charge (Q), coulomb (C), nanocoulomb (nC)

slo.purpose: Learners rub pairs of materials together, use the repulsion test to find the sign of charge on each, and use the triboelectric table to explain that friction transfers electrons so the balloon becomes negative and the hair positive.
slo.knowledge: Friction transfers electrons from one material to another. Protons stay in the nucleus. The sign of charge depends on the pair of materials (triboelectric order: dry human hair (+), glass, perspex, wool/fur, silk, polythene, ebonite, latex balloon (-)). The material higher in the list becomes positive when rubbed with one lower in the list. Charge is not created: the two materials gain equal and opposite charge and total charge is conserved. A rubbed balloon gains about 1 nC, about 6 x 10^9 extra electrons, out of roughly 10^23 atoms.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (particle-level diagrams of electron transfer); planning and carrying out investigations (rubbing pairs, repulsion test); analysing and interpreting data (ranking materials, finding patterns in a table); using mathematics (charge in nC to number of electrons); constructing explanations.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about invisible forces; honesty in recording results even when they differ from predictions; cooperation in groups; respect for evidence; care when handling materials. Learners value careful observation and using evidence to revise their models.
slo.keyInquiry: Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects? (Focus: What happens to the electrons when two materials are rubbed together, and which material ends up positive or negative?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 gave us the puzzling observations: hair rises, the balloon sticks to the wall and paper jumps. Lesson 2 gave us the tools: protons (+), electrons (-), neutrons (0), neutral atoms, and the rule that like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Lesson 3 answers the first part of the driving question: where charges come from. Learners find that charge is not created but transferred as electrons by friction, and they assign the balloon as negative and the hair as positive. This provides the transfer mechanism that Lessons 4, 5 and 6 will build on (conductors, contact, and induction explaining the neutral wall and paper).
slo.safetyNotes: Use only dry, clean materials and low-energy rubbing; no mains electricity or high-voltage equipment. Keep balloons away from eyes and do not put them over the mouth. Check for latex allergy before the balloon activity and offer a polythene strip instead. Hang threads from desk edges or retort stands, not from the ceiling. Keep the stations tidy so learners do not trip over threads. A mild shock from a jersey is harmless, but learners should not deliberately try to shock others.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Mwangi opens with the hair and balloon from Lesson 1 and asks: what is the balloon taking from, or giving to, the hair? Learners predict, then rotate through stations rubbing polythene, perspex, ebonite, glass, silk, fur and a latex balloon in pairs. Each rubbed object is hung on a thread and tested with the Lesson 2 repulsion test against a known negative polythene strip (rubbed with wool/fur) and a known positive perspex rod (rubbed with silk). From the class data they build a triboelectric order and compare it with the official table. In the Explain phase they draw particle-level models of electron transfer for the balloon and hair, check that total charge is conserved, and calculate that 1 nC is about 6 x 10^9 electrons, a tiny fraction of the roughly 10^23 atoms in a balloon. They add new questions to the DQB (why does the balloon stick to the neutral wall? Why does it fail in Mombasa's humidity?) and revise their initial models from Lesson 1.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the balloon and hair from Lesson 1 (20 strokes, hair rises up to 5 cm). On a prediction card they answer individually: (1) After rubbing, is the balloon charged? Is the hair? (2) What do you think moved between them? (3) If the balloon is negative, what sign is the hair? Wanjiru says her hair rises after combing on dry Nairobi mornings; learners predict whether the comb and her hair have the same or opposite charge. Then, in pairs, they predict which material, polythene or perspex, will become positive when rubbed with silk, and explain why. They record predictions in their notebooks with a sketch of their current idea.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up a latex balloon and a lock of hair. Say: "Last week the balloon made hair rise. Today we ask a more precise question: what exactly happened to the hair and to the balloon when I rubbed them?" Give 2 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: "What do you think moved from one to the other, if anything?" Cold-call 4 learners, including at least one who has not spoken yet. Record every prediction on the board, without evaluating, in three columns: 'Charge is made', 'Something moves', 'Not sure'. Ask: "Wanjiru, does your comb make charge, or take it from your hair? How could we test that?" Do not reveal electrons yet; use Lesson 2 vocabulary (protons +, electrons -, neutrons 0) and ask learners which particles could possibly move in a solid.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Eliciting prior ideas through Predict-Explain: learners commit to a prediction and a reason before seeing data. Making ideas public surfaces the common misconception that rubbing creates charge, so the later evidence has something to confront and learners can see how their thinking changes.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) learners who say 'rubbing creates charge' versus 'charge moves'; (b) whether they apply the Lesson 2 rule that like charges repel and unlike charges attract; (c) whether they name electrons as the particles most likely to move. Tally the three columns of the board; target at least 70% of learners giving a reason, not just a guess. Note learners who say positive charge moves, to address in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners rotate through 3 stations (about 8 minutes each). Station A (Known signs): rub a polythene strip with wool/fur and a perspex rod with silk, hang each on a thread, and confirm that two polythene strips repel, two perspex rods repel and polythene and perspex attract (Lesson 2 results), giving a negative reference (polythene) and positive reference (perspex). Station B (Pairs): rub each pair with 20 strokes: glass with silk, ebonite with fur, perspex with wool/fur, polythene with silk, and a balloon with dry hair. Test each rubbed object against both references. Only repulsion counts as proof of sign; attraction alone could be a neutral object. Record in a table: material, repelled by polythene or perspex, sign. Station C (Both partners): test that the cloth also becomes charged, with the opposite sign to the rod, by hanging the cloth or hair and testing it. Learners also test an unrubbed object as a control, which should show no repulsion. Finally, the class pools results and ranks the materials into an order from most positive to most negative.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the stations, say: "Attraction is not enough. A neutral object is also attracted to a charged one. Which result proves the sign?" WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 2 learners to say 'repulsion'. While circulating ask: "Which one repelled the polythene? What sign does that make it?" and "Did the cloth gain the same sign as the rod or the opposite?" Prompt: "Why did you test an unrubbed object?" Remind groups of 20 strokes each and a dry surface; if a group gets weak results, ask: "What could be different about the air or the materials?" (link to Amina's Mombasa humidity). Keep reference rods away from other materials so they stay charged. After the stations, collect results on a class chart and ask 3 groups to report, cold-calling a different learner in each. Ask: "Where does the balloon-hair pair fit in the order? Which one is higher?" Show the triboelectric table only after learners have their own order: dry human hair (+), glass, perspex, wool/fur, silk, polythene, ebonite, latex balloon (-).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data pattern-finding with a class results table: learners compare their observed order with the table and look for the pattern that the material higher in the list becomes positive and the one lower becomes negative. Using a controlled test (unrubbed control, two references) builds the reasoning that repulsion is the reliable sign test.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: learners use repulsion, not attraction, as the evidence for sign; the table has a sign for every material with a stated reason; groups find that the rod and cloth have opposite signs; the class order roughly matches the triboelectric table. Check that the balloon is recorded as negative and hair as positive. Ask each group to show one row of evidence (e.g. 'perspex repelled perspex, so it is positive'). Note any group that reports attraction as proof of sign for re-teaching.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their data to explain why the balloon becomes negative and the hair positive. Step 1: they draw a particle-level diagram of the hair and balloon before rubbing (both neutral: equal + and - symbols). Step 2: they draw after rubbing: the balloon has extra electrons (-), the hair has a deficit (+), with an arrow showing electrons moving from hair to balloon. They explain why the hair strands, now both positive, repel each other and rise, and why they are attracted to the negative balloon (Lesson 1 and 2 rule). Step 3: charge conservation: they count symbols to show the total is the same before and after (e.g. 6 electrons moved: balloon -6, hair +6, total 0). Step 4: a calculation: a balloon gains about 1 nC; number of electrons = 1 x 10^-9 / 1.6 x 10^-19 = 6.25 x 10^9, about 6 x 10^9, compared to about 10^23 atoms in the balloon, so only a tiny fraction of electrons move. Kipchoge asks if the shock from a jersey is like lightning, and learners explain that the jersey and body exchange electrons by friction and the built-up charge discharges as a small spark on a dry Nairobi day (35% humidity).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Use evidence from today's table. Why is the balloon negative and the hair positive?" WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then pair-share for 2 minutes. Cold-call 3 pairs. Press for precision: "Which particles moved? Did protons move? Why not?" (they are in the nucleus). Correct any statement of 'positive charge moved' with: "In a solid, only electrons move. Positive means a deficit of electrons." Ask: "Latex holds electrons more strongly than hair; where is that on our table?" Model the calculation on the board, then ask learners to do it for 2 nC. Ask: "If the balloon gains 6 x 10^9 electrons, how many does the hair lose?" (the same number, so charge is conserved). Ask: "Is charge created or transferred?" Do not explain why the balloon sticks to the wall or the paper jumps; say: "That is a new question for the DQB. We will need induction later." Do not discuss conductors or contact charging, which are for Lessons 4 and 5. Invite Kipchoge's question into the discussion and say lightning will be handled in Lesson 7.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Modelling with particle-level diagrams and a claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) frame: Claim (balloon is negative, hair positive), Evidence (repulsion tests, table), Reasoning (electron transfer, conservation of charge). Drawing before and after states makes the invisible transfer concrete, and the calculation shows the scale of the transfer.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: diagrams where electrons, not protons, move; equal and opposite charge on balloon and hair; a total of zero before and after; correct calculation of 6 x 10^9 electrons for 1 nC and a correct scaled answer for 2 nC (about 1.25 x 10^10); correct use of 'transfer' not 'create'; the CER statement that cites repulsion evidence. Use a quick exit check: 'Hair is positive because it has... (a deficit of electrons).' Aim for at least 80% correct. Note learners who say positive charges moved.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB from Lesson 1. In groups they write on sticky notes: (1) a question now answered (e.g. 'Does rubbing make charge?'), with the evidence from today, and move it to the 'Answered' section; (2) new questions raised by today's work (e.g. 'Why does the balloon stick to the neutral wall if the wall has no charge?', 'Why did Amina's balloon not work in Mombasa's rainy season?', 'Why do some materials, like metal, not hold charge when rubbed?', 'Is the jersey shock like lightning?'). They sort questions by lesson ('Where do charges come from?' is now mostly answered; 'How do we detect charge?' and 'Why does charge stay on the balloon?' remain open).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at the DQB. Which of our questions can we now answer with today's evidence?" WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to move a note and give the evidence. Then ask: "What new questions do you have?" Cold-call 3 more learners. Ask: "Otieno, you saw the balloon stick to the wall; does today's rubbing explain the wall?" and guide them to see that the wall was not rubbed and so needs another explanation (a link to later lessons). Do not answer open questions; label them with the likely lesson (conductors in Lesson 4, contact in Lesson 5, induction and the wall in Lesson 6, points and lightning in Lesson 7). Photograph the DQB.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of understanding: moving questions to 'answered' with cited evidence shows progress, and the new questions create a need to know that motivates the following lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: at least one question per group is moved to 'Answered' with a piece of evidence; new questions are specific and linked to the phenomenon (wall, paper, humidity, shock); at least two groups identify the wall question as unexplained by friction. Check that learners do not claim 'answered' without evidence.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the model they began in Lesson 1 and updated in Lesson 2: a labelled particle-level diagram of the balloon, hair, wall and paper. In this lesson they add: the balloon with excess electrons (-), the hair with a deficit (+) and an arrow for electrons moving from hair to balloon, the label '~1 nC = ~6 x 10^9 electrons', and a note that total charge is conserved. They draw the hair strands repelling each other and being attracted to the balloon. For the wall and paper, they draw them neutral, with a question mark and the note 'Why attracted? (Lesson 6)'. They write a 2-3 sentence caption using 'transfer of electrons' and finish the summary table.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Revise your model with today's evidence. Show the electrons moving. Label the signs." Circulate and ask: "Where did the electrons come from? Where did they go? Is the total charge the same?" WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 3 learners to explain one part of their model. Say: "Keep the wall and paper neutral for now. Mark what you cannot yet explain." Insist on correct vocabulary: 'electrons are transferred', not 'charge is made'. Collect models for review. Preview Lesson 4: "Why does the charge stay on the balloon? Why does it not stay on a metal spoon? We will test that next time."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Iterative model revision with gaps made explicit: learners add new evidence and mark the parts the model cannot yet explain (wall, paper, humidity), so models are treated as tools that improve as evidence grows.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check models for: electron arrow from hair to balloon; balloon negative and hair positive; equal numbers of transferred charges; the 1 nC and 6 x 10^9 label; hair strands repelling; wall and paper neutral and flagged as unexplained; no protons shown moving. Success: at least 80% of models include all of these. Use the caption for individual feedback.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask: Did learners use repulsion, not attraction, as evidence of sign? Did anyone still say charge was 'made' or that positive charges moved? Which groups had weak results, and was humidity or damp materials the cause? Did the table pattern emerge from their data before I showed the official triboelectric table? Did the calculation (1 nC to 6 x 10^9 electrons out of 10^23 atoms) help them see the scale? Were quieter learners heard during the cold-calls? Did I resist explaining the wall and paper, leaving that to Lesson 6? What should I change in the Lesson 4 conductor investigation so that learners connect free electrons to why the balloon holds charge?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We rubbed pairs of materials (glass with silk, ebonite with fur, perspex with wool/fur, polythene with silk, balloon with hair) and tested them against a negative polythene strip and a positive perspex rod. Rod and cloth had opposite signs, shown by repulsion. The balloon was negative and the hair positive. Unrubbed objects showed no effect.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Friction transfers electrons from one material to the other. Protons stay in the nucleus. The sign depends on the material pair, following the triboelectric order: dry human hair (+), glass, perspex, wool/fur, silk, polythene, ebonite, latex balloon (-). Charge is conserved: the balloon gains about 1 nC (6 x 10^9 electrons) and the hair loses the same amount, out of about 10^23 atoms.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: When I rub the balloon on my hair, electrons transfer from the hair to the balloon because latex holds electrons more strongly. The balloon becomes negative and the hair positive. The hair strands, all positive, repel each other and rise, and they are attracted to the negative balloon. Charge is not created. Still to explain: why the balloon sticks to the neutral wall and attracts paper, and why humidity makes it fail.

LESSONS.title: Conductors and Insulators: Why Does the Balloon Keep Its Charge While a Metal Spoon Does Not?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: conductor, insulator, free electrons, delocalised electrons, simple circuit, bulb, cell, electron transfer, electric charge

slo.purpose: Learners test materials in a simple circuit to separate conductors from insulators, and use free (delocalised) electrons to explain why the rubbed latex balloon keeps its charge and sticks to the wall.
slo.knowledge: Conductors (copper, aluminium, steel spoon, graphite) have free (delocalised) electrons that move through the material. Insulators (plastic, dry wood, rubber, glass, dry cotton) hold their electrons tightly bound. Only electrons move in solids; protons stay in the nucleus.
slo.skills: Planning and carrying out an investigation (NGSS SEP 3): build a circuit with a 3 V cell pair and torch bulb, test 9 materials and record bulb lit or not lit. Developing and using models (SEP 2): draw particle-level diagrams of free versus bound electrons. Constructing explanations (SEP 6).
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about invisible particles, honesty in recording results even when they surprise, safe and careful handling of circuits, and respect for each other's ideas during discussion.
slo.keyInquiry: Why do some materials conduct electricity while others don't?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 2 and 3 showed that electrons are the movers and that friction transfers them to the balloon. Learners now ask why the balloon's charge stays on it instead of spreading away. This lesson gives the idea of free versus bound electrons that is needed for contact charging (Lesson 5), induction and earthing (Lesson 6) and distribution of charge (Lesson 7).
slo.safetyNotes: Use only the 3 V supply (two 1.5 V cells in series). Never connect to mains sockets. Do not short-circuit the cells with bare wire for more than a few seconds because wire and cells heat up. Keep spoons and wires away from the face. Wash hands after handling graphite and metals. Keep all materials dry; teachers always use dry conditions.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Mwangi reopens the balloon phenomenon: the rubbed balloon stays charged and sticks to the wall for about 3 minutes on a dry Nairobi day, but a metal spoon rubbed with wool never seems to hold charge. Learners predict which of 9 materials will light a bulb, build a circuit with a 3 V cell pair and torch bulb, and test copper wire, aluminium foil, a steel spoon, graphite, a plastic ruler, dry wood, rubber, a glass rod and dry cotton cloth. They sort results, explain them with free versus tightly bound electrons, and revise the DQB and their particle-level model to show why charge stays put on the insulating latex balloon. Contact charging, induction and earthing are left for Lessons 5 and 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Mr Mwangi holds up a rubbed balloon stuck to the wall and recalls Otieno's observation from Kisumu that it stays for about 3 minutes. He then holds a steel spoon and asks, 'If electrons moved onto the balloon from the hair, why do they stay put on the balloon?' Learners individually write a prediction for 9 materials (copper wire, aluminium foil, steel spoon, graphite pencil lead, plastic ruler, dry wood, rubber, glass rod, dry cotton cloth): will the bulb light in a circuit with a 3 V cell pair, Yes or No? They give a one-line reason, then share in pairs and mark their predictions on a class tally on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last lesson we learned that friction transfers electrons to the balloon. Today we ask: what lets electrons move through some materials but not others?' Ask: 'Which of these 9 materials do you think will let electricity pass? Write Yes or No and a reason.' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds of silent writing before any talk. Give pairs 2 minutes. Cold-call 4 learners (e.g. Amina, Kipchoge, Wanjiru, Otieno) for one prediction each and the reason, and record on the board without judging. Ask: 'Who changed their mind after hearing a partner?' Do not reveal answers.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with a class tally: committing to written predictions before evidence creates cognitive conflict when results surprise learners, and the recorded reasons expose preconceptions (for example, that all metals or all solids conduct, or that wood conducts) that the evidence can then test.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that 100% of learners have written 9 predictions with at least 3 reasons. Look for reasons using ideas from Lessons 2 and 3 (electrons move, protons stay). Note the number of learners predicting that plastic or wood conducts, and the number who mention 'metal' only as a reason. Record the tally for comparison after the test.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners build a simple circuit with two 1.5 V cells in series (3 V), a torch bulb and connecting wires, leaving a gap. They touch the gap ends to each material in turn: copper wire, aluminium foil, metal (steel) spoon, graphite (pencil lead), plastic ruler, dry wood, rubber, glass rod, dry cotton cloth. Results: the bulb lights with copper wire, aluminium foil, steel spoon and graphite; it does not light with plastic ruler, dry wood, rubber, glass rod or dry cotton cloth. They record bulb Lit or Not lit in a table, compare with their predictions, and mark each as conductor or insulator. They then link back to the phenomenon: the balloon is latex rubber, which does not light the bulb.
framework.teacherMoves: Demonstrate one safe circuit with copper first, then circulate. Say: 'Make sure the material completes the gap, with both ends firmly touching.' Ask: 'What would a bulb that does not light tell you? Is the circuit broken, or is the material not letting electrons pass?' Tell groups to first test the bulb by touching the two wire ends together. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before groups record each result to allow them to check contacts. Prompt: 'Which result surprised your group? Is graphite a metal?' Ask each group to retest any 'odd' result once. Remind: 'Keep materials dry. A damp cloth could give a different result.' Cold-call 3 groups to report the two materials they tested last.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data table with pattern-finding (SEP 3 and SEP 4): recording lit or not lit for all 9 materials makes a consistent pattern visible, and retesting odd results teaches reliability of evidence. Graphite is a key case because it is not a metal, so a 'metals conduct' rule is not enough and learners need a mechanism.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether groups complete the circuit correctly and test the bulb first. Check that all 9 results are recorded with 4 materials lit and 5 not lit. Look for correct use of the words conductor and insulator. Note groups that retest an unexpected result rather than changing it to match their prediction.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sort the 9 materials into conductors (copper, aluminium, steel spoon, graphite) and insulators (plastic ruler, dry wood, rubber, glass, dry cotton). Using a model of a metal as a lattice of fixed positive ions surrounded by free (delocalised) electrons, they draw how electrons drift through a conductor from the negative terminal of the cell, and how in an insulator electrons stay tightly bound to their atoms. In pairs they write a 3-sentence explanation: why does the bulb light with the steel spoon but not with the plastic ruler? Then they apply it to the balloon: because latex is an insulator, the extra electrons gained from the hair (about 6 x 10^9 for 1 nC) cannot move through the balloon and stay where they were deposited, so the balloon keeps its charge and stays stuck to the wall for about 3 minutes on a dry day.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Only electrons move in solids; protons stay in the nucleus.' Ask: 'What is different about the electrons in copper and in the plastic ruler?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to describe free electrons in their own words, and 2 more to challenge or add. Ask: 'Graphite is not a metal. What does its bulb result tell us about its electrons?' Draw the two particle diagrams on the board while learners draw theirs. Ask: 'Why do we say a conductor has free electrons, not free protons?' Then ask: 'Why does the extra charge on the rubbed balloon stay on the balloon?' Do not teach charging by contact or earthing; say: 'Lesson 5 will ask what happens when a charged object touches a conductor.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Modelling with particle-level diagrams and Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (SEP 2 and 6): claim (steel spoon is a conductor), evidence (bulb lit), reasoning (free electrons move through the material). Drawing bound versus free electrons links the observable bulb result to the invisible particle explanation, and applying it to the balloon connects it to the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each pair's explanation for three indicators: (1) says electrons, not protons, move; (2) says conductors have free or delocalised electrons and insulators have tightly bound electrons; (3) links the latex balloon being an insulator to the charge staying on it. Ask learners to hold up fingers (1-3) for how many indicators they included. Flag learners who say charge is created or that positive charge moves in solids.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB from Lesson 1. They add sticky notes with (a) answers they now have, such as 'Rubber balloons are insulators, so the electrons stay on them' and (b) new questions such as 'If metals let electrons move, can we charge a spoon?' (Kipchoge), 'Why did my hair stand up less in humid Mombasa?' (Amina), and 'Would a metal balloon hold charge?' (Otieno). They group notes under KICD questions 2 (What are electric charges?) and 3 (Why do some materials conduct and others don't?), and mark questions to be answered in Lessons 5 to 8.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Choose one question you can now partly answer and one new question we cannot answer yet.' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds for writing. Cold-call 4 learners to read a note and place it on the board. Ask: 'Which earlier question does the conductor-insulator idea help with?' Ask the class to tell you whether each new question is about contact, induction, distribution or detecting charge, and tag it with the matching lesson number. Keep Amina's humidity question open and ask: 'What might water vapour do to charge on an insulator?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with question-clustering: sorting notes shows learners how the evidence builds toward the driving question and how their own questions shape upcoming lessons, which keeps learners as owners of the inquiry.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count the notes: aim for at least 1 new answer and 1 new question per learner. Check that answers use free or bound electrons correctly. Look for questions that point forward (contact, induction, earthing, spreading of charge) as evidence of curiosity and understanding of the sequence.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise their labelled particle-level model of the balloon, hair, wall and paper. They add: (1) the balloon as an insulating latex surface where the extra electrons (about 6 x 10^9 for 1 nC out of roughly 10^23 atoms) stay in place; (2) hair as positive; (3) a note that the wall and paper have electrons that are tightly bound but can shift slightly, which they will test in Lesson 6. They add an arrow labelled 'a metal spoon would let electrons move' and a caption 'Latex is an insulator: electrons stay where friction put them.' They write one sentence explaining why the balloon sticks for about 3 minutes on a dry day.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use a different colour to add today's idea to your Lesson 3 model. Show only what the evidence supports.' Ask: 'Where on your model are the free electrons? Where are the bound electrons?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before pairs compare. Cold-call 3 learners to explain their revised diagram. Say: 'We have not yet explained why the wall attracts the paper; leave that gap labelled with a question mark.' Ask: 'What can your model not yet explain?' Collect models for review.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Iterative model revision (SEP 2): adding a new layer of explanation in a different colour makes the growth of understanding visible, and labelling the gaps with question marks identifies what later lessons must explain, so the model becomes a tool for prediction and not just illustration.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each model for: electrons shown on the balloon, a label saying latex is an insulator, protons not moving, and a clearly marked unexplained gap. Look for correct signs (balloon negative, hair positive). Note any learner who shows positive charges moving in the solid and revisit it in a short conference.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners explained conductors using free electrons rather than just saying 'metals conduct'? Did graphite help to move learners beyond the rule 'metals conduct'? Did anyone say that an insulator cannot be charged, and how did you address it with the balloon? Which predictions changed most after the circuit test? Which DQB questions should be prioritised in Lesson 5 and Lesson 6? Were all tests done in dry conditions, and did any result differ because of damp materials?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: The bulb lit with copper wire, aluminium foil, a steel spoon and graphite. It did not light with a plastic ruler, dry wood, rubber, a glass rod or dry cotton cloth in the 3 V circuit.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Conductors have free (delocalised) electrons that can move through the material; insulators have tightly bound electrons. Only electrons move in solids. The latex balloon is an insulator, so the electrons it gains from the hair stay on it.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The balloon is negative and holds its extra electrons (about 6 x 10^9 for 1 nC) because latex is an insulator, so the charge cannot move away and the balloon stays charged and sticks for about 3 minutes on a dry day.
