LESSONS.title: Charging by Contact: Why Do Paper Pieces Touch the Balloon and Then Fall Off?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: charging by contact, conductor, electron transfer, same sign of charge, gold-leaf electroscope, leaf divergence, electrostatic force, conservation of charge

slo.purpose: Learners investigate what happens when a conductor is touched by a charged object, so that they can explain the sign of charge the conductor gains using electron movement. This advances the driving question by explaining why paper pieces that touch the balloon later fall off.
slo.knowledge: A conductor touched by a charged object gains the SAME sign of charge by transfer of electrons. A negative polythene strip touched to the electroscope cap leaves the leaf at about 30 degrees after the strip is removed. Electrons move because conductors have free electrons (Lesson 4). Charge is transferred, not created (Lesson 3).
slo.skills: Developing and using models (particle-level diagrams of electron transfer); planning and carrying out investigations (electroscope observations); analysing and interpreting data (leaf divergence in degrees before, during and after contact); constructing explanations using evidence; communicating in pairs and groups.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about invisible forces; careful, honest observation and recording; respect for others' ideas during discussion; perseverance when a result is unexpected; safe handling of equipment.
slo.keyInquiry: How can we charge conductors? (links to the driving question: Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 3 and 4 showed that friction transfers electrons and that conductors have free electrons. Lesson 5 asks what happens when a charged object TOUCHES a conductor. It explains why paper pieces that touch the balloon sometimes fall off, and gives the rule that contact gives the SAME sign. Lesson 6 will contrast this with induction, which gives the OPPOSITE sign.
slo.safetyNotes: Use only dry, low-charge equipment (polythene strip rubbed with wool, 20 strokes). The charges are very small and harmless. Handle the gold-leaf electroscope gently because the leaf is fragile, and do not breathe or blow on it. Keep the equipment dry, because humidity makes the charge leak away. Tidy away torn paper and cloths after the lesson.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Mwangi reminds the class of the puzzle from Lesson 1: some paper pieces jumped up to the rubbed balloon, touched it, and then fell off. Learners first predict what will happen to a neutral electroscope when a negative polythene strip touches its cap. They then observe the leaf rise to about 30 degrees and stay there after the strip is removed, and they watch paper pieces behave in the same way at the balloon. In the Explain phase they use free electrons (Lesson 4) and electron transfer (Lesson 3) to explain that the cap, stem and leaf gained extra electrons and so became negative, the same sign as the strip. They connect this to the paper pieces: after touching the negative balloon, a piece gains the same sign, so it is repelled and falls off. The class updates the Driving Question Board and revises the particle-level model of the balloon, hair, wall and paper.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the balloon on the wall and the paper pieces that jumped to the balloon and then fell off (Lesson 1). Mr Mwangi shows a neutral gold-leaf electroscope with the leaf hanging at 0 degrees and a rubbed polythene strip (negative, from Lesson 2). Individually, in their notebooks, learners predict what will happen to the leaf if the strip is touched to the cap and then removed. They sketch the leaf before, during and after contact and write one sentence of reasoning. They then compare predictions with a partner. Wanjiru predicts that the leaf will only rise while the strip is there. Otieno predicts that it will stay up.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Remember the paper pieces that jumped up to the balloon and then fell off again. Today we find out why." Hold up the neutral electroscope and point to the leaf at 0 degrees. Ask: "If I touch this negative strip to the cap and then take it away, what will the leaf do? Sketch it before, during and after." Give 2 minutes of silent individual writing. WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds after asking for reasoning before taking any answers. Then cold-call 3 learners (for example Wanjiru, Otieno and Amina) to share a prediction and a reason, and record the predictions in 3 columns on the board: "falls back to 0 degrees", "stays up", "goes higher". Do not say which is correct.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction stage): committing to a written prediction with a reason makes learners' current ideas about charge visible. It sets up cognitive conflict if the leaf does not fall back after the strip is removed, so learners need to revise their thinking in the later phases.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for learners who: (1) sketch three separate leaf positions (before, during, after); (2) give a reason that mentions electrons, charge or the strip, not only "it just moves"; (3) use the term 'leaf divergence' or 'leaf rises' correctly. Note on a class list who predicts that the leaf returns to 0 degrees after removal, because this shows the idea that charge only stays while the charged object is near. Count how many learners mention electrons in their reasoning (aim for at least 5 of 10 in a quick scan).

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, with a gold-leaf electroscope, a polythene strip and a wool or fur cloth per group (Mr Mwangi demonstrates first), learners: (1) check that the leaf is at 0 degrees; (2) rub the polythene strip with wool for 20 strokes (negative, from Lesson 2); (3) bring the strip near the cap without touching: the leaf rises to about 30 degrees and falls back when the strip is taken away; (4) discharge the electroscope by touching the cap with a finger; (5) touch the strip to the cap, then remove the strip: the leaf stays at about 30 degrees. Learners record leaf divergence in degrees in a table: neutral 0 degrees, strip near (not touching) about 30 degrees, after touching and removing about 30 degrees, after finger touch 0 degrees. Then, in a quick demonstration, Mr Mwangi holds a rubbed balloon (dry conditions) 2 cm above torn paper pieces: they jump to the balloon, and some fall off again after touching it. Learners record which pieces fall off, and when.
framework.teacherMoves: Model the first trial slowly while the groups watch. Say: "Eyes on the leaf, not the strip. Read the angle at the protractor scale and record it in degrees." Circulate and ask each group: "What is the leaf doing now that the strip has gone?" Stress the difference between near but not touching, and touching. If a group's leaf falls quickly, say: "Check that your strip and the electroscope are dry, and that you rubbed for 20 strokes." Remind learners that the leaf is fragile and must not be breathed on. For the paper demonstration say: "Watch a paper piece. It jumps up, touches, and then... what happens?" WAIT TIME: after the demonstration, wait 10-15 seconds in silence before taking observations. Cold-call 4 groups to report one measurement each, and record the class data on the board in a table.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data collection with a comparison table: recording leaf divergence in degrees under different conditions (near, touching, finger earthing) lets learners see patterns. They notice that touching leaves the leaf at about 30 degrees, the same as when the strip was near, but the charge stays after the strip is removed. Linking the electroscope result to the paper pieces moves learners from a lab observation to the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that group tables show: neutral 0 degrees; strip near about 30 degrees; after touching and removing about 30 degrees; after finger 0 degrees. Observable indicators: learners read angles in degrees (not "high" or "low"); learners notice the difference between the leaf falling back when the strip is only near and staying up after contact; learners state in their own words that the paper pieces that fell off had touched the balloon. Ask 3 learners: "What is different between near and touching?" and listen for "the charge stayed" or "something moved onto the electroscope".

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in their groups to explain the observations. Using Lesson 4 (conductors have free electrons) and Lesson 3 (friction transfers electrons), they answer: (1) Where did the extra electrons on the polythene strip come from? (2) When the negative strip touched the metal cap, what could the free electrons do? (3) Why does the leaf stay at about 30 degrees after the strip is removed? (4) What sign of charge does the electroscope now have? Each group draws a particle-level diagram in three steps: before contact (neutral cap, stem and leaf), during contact (electrons moving from the strip onto the cap and spreading down to the leaf), and after (electroscope with excess electrons, leaf and stem repelling each other). Learners then use the rule: contact gives the SAME sign as the charged object. They apply it to the paper pieces: a neutral paper piece is first attracted to the negative balloon, touches it, gains some electrons, becomes negative, and is then repelled and falls off. Kipchoge asks whether the cap gets positive because the leaf moves: the class uses the repulsion test, with the leaf rising further when a negative object is brought near, to answer.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Use only electrons moving. Protons stay in the nucleus." Ask: "When the strip touched the cap, which way did the electrons move, and why did they spread to the leaf?" WAIT TIME: give 10-15 seconds of silent thinking before groups discuss. Then ask learners to turn to a partner for 2 minutes. Cold-call 3 pairs to explain one step each (before, during, after). Correct any phrase like "positive charge moved" with: "In a solid, only electrons move. Say it again using electrons." Ask: "Why do the stem and leaf both become negative? What do like charges do?" Use the answer "the leaf and stem repel each other, so the leaf rises". Then ask: "Now think about the paper piece that touched the balloon. What sign does it have now, and what happens?" Finish by writing the rule on the board: "Contact gives the SAME sign. Electrons are transferred, not created." Ask: "If we count the extra electrons on the balloon, about 6 x 10^9 (Lesson 3), does the balloon lose any when the paper touches it?" Guide them to say: a few move to the paper, and total charge is conserved.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with particle-level modelling: learners make the claim 'the electroscope gained the same (negative) sign', support it with the 30 degrees leaf divergence that remains after removal, and give reasoning with free electrons and like charges repelling. Drawing a three-step before/during/after diagram makes the invisible electron transfer visible and transfers to the paper pieces.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for diagrams that: show electrons (not protons) moving from the strip to the cap; show extra electrons spread to the leaf and stem; label the electroscope as negative afterwards; use the words 'transfer' and 'same sign'. Listen for correct reasoning that the leaf rises because the like (negative) charges repel. Common errors to note: 'the strip's charge was used up', 'positive charges moved', or 'the electroscope became positive'. Ask an exit question: "A positive perspex rod touches a neutral electroscope. What sign does it gain, and which way do electrons move?" Expect: positive, electrons move from the electroscope to the rod.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1. Working in groups, they write on sticky notes (a) one question they can now answer, with evidence from today (for example, 'Why did the paper pieces fall off the balloon? Because they touched and gained the same negative charge, and like charges repel'), and (b) one new question that today's evidence raises (for example, 'Why is the neutral paper attracted to the balloon in the first place?', 'What if the electroscope were touched with a finger?' or 'How can we get the OPPOSITE sign on a conductor?'). They place the notes on the DQB under the headings 'Answered', 'Partly answered' and 'New questions'. Amina adds a note linking humidity to the charge leaking away from the electroscope.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at our board. Which of our questions can we now answer with evidence from today?" Give each group 3 minutes to write notes. WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds after asking for a new question so that learners think before writing. Cold-call 3 groups to read a note aloud and say where it should go. Point out the questions about attraction of neutral paper and the wall, and say: "We will return to these in the next lesson, when we look at charging by induction and earthing." Move the question 'Where do electric charges come from?' to 'Partly answered' and ask: "What do we know now about where the charge comes from?"
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with 'Answered / Partly answered / New questions': sorting questions against evidence shows learners how their understanding is growing and gives them ownership of the investigation. It keeps the unit coherent from lesson to lesson and motivates Lesson 6.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each group's answered note cites evidence (such as 'leaf stayed at about 30 degrees after the strip was removed') and not just a statement. Check that new questions are testable or linked to the phenomenon. Indicators of progress: at least 3 notes use the words electrons, transfer or same sign correctly; at least 1 group asks about the attraction of neutral objects, which leads to induction in Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out the particle-level model of the balloon, hair, wall and paper they have been building since Lesson 1. Individually, they revise it by adding: (1) a paper piece near the negative balloon being attracted; (2) the same paper piece touching the balloon, with a few electrons shown moving from the balloon onto the paper; (3) the paper piece now negative and repelled, falling off. They label the balloon as negative (excess of electrons), the hair as positive (deficit of electrons), and use arrows for electron movement and for the electrostatic force. They add a short caption: 'Contact gives the SAME sign. Electrons are transferred, not created.' Then they complete a short summary of the model changes with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Revise your model from last lesson. Add today's idea: what happens when the paper touches the balloon?" Circulate and prompt: "Which particles moved? Which way? What sign does the paper have afterwards? What does the paper do next?" Insist that balloon is negative and hair is positive. WAIT TIME: allow 10-15 seconds of silent thinking before learners start to draw. Cold-call 3 learners to explain one change in their model, and ask a different learner to say whether they agree and why. Ask: "What is still missing from our model?" Guide them to say that it does not yet explain why the NEUTRAL paper was attracted before touching, which is Lesson 6. Collect the models to check.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Iterative model revision with peer critique: learners add today's evidence to the same model rather than starting again. Revising the model shows how scientific explanations change with new evidence, and peer explanations check that the model really accounts for the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that revised models: show electrons (not protons) moving between balloon and paper; label the paper as negative after contact; show repulsion as the reason for falling off; keep the balloon negative and hair positive; and show gaps honestly (attraction of neutral paper unexplained). A learner meets the target if they can say, using the model: 'The paper touched the balloon, gained electrons, became negative like the balloon, and was repelled.' Record who needs support with direction of electron movement.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners still believed that charge disappears when the strip is removed or that positive charge moves in solids, and how did the three-step particle diagram change their thinking? Did the electroscope result (about 30 degrees remaining after contact) create a real surprise for the class, and did learners connect it to the paper pieces that fell off the balloon? Were dry conditions kept, and if some groups' leaves fell quickly, did that lead to a useful humidity discussion (Mombasa, about 80%, compared with Nairobi, about 35%)? Which questions on the DQB should be used to open Lesson 6, and who needs more support to contrast the SAME sign (contact) with the OPPOSITE sign (induction) next time?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: The leaf of a neutral electroscope stayed at about 30 degrees after a negative polythene strip touched the cap and was removed (0 degrees before; about 30 degrees also when the strip was only near). Touching the cap with a finger returned the leaf to 0 degrees. Paper pieces jumped up to the rubbed balloon and some fell off again after touching it.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: A conductor touched by a charged object gains the SAME sign of charge by transfer of electrons. Free electrons in the conductor let the charge spread to the leaf, and like charges repel, so the leaf stays raised. Charge is transferred, not created.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The negative strip passed extra electrons to the cap, stem and leaf, so they all became negative and repelled each other. In the same way, a paper piece that touches the negative balloon gains electrons, becomes negative, and is repelled, so it falls off. This adds one more step to the balloon-and-hair explanation, though why neutral paper is attracted at first is still to be explained.

LESSONS.title: Charging by Induction and Earthing: Charging Without Touching
LESSONS.aresKeywords: induction, charge separation, earthing, opposite sign, electroscope, leaf divergence, neutral, electron transfer

slo.purpose: Learners explain how a charged object can attract a neutral object by induction, and show how a conductor can be given the OPPOSITE sign of charge using induction and earthing. This explains why the neutral wall and paper are attracted to the negative balloon.
slo.knowledge: Induction is the separation of charge in a neutral object when a charged object is brought near without touching. In a conductor, free electrons move away from a negative object (or toward a positive one), leaving the near side with the opposite sign. In an insulator such as paper or a painted wall, electrons shift only slightly within their atoms. Attraction is stronger than repulsion because the opposite charge is nearer. Charging by induction needs earthing and gives the OPPOSITE sign to the charged object (contact gives the SAME sign). Earthing lets electrons flow to or from the Earth.
slo.skills: Predicting and observing with a gold-leaf electroscope; measuring leaf divergence in degrees; developing and using particle-level models (NGSS SEP 2); analysing and interpreting data (SEP 4); constructing explanations (SEP 6); using evidence to compare contact and induction.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about invisible forces; honesty in reporting observations, including surprises; careful and safe handling of apparatus; respect for peers' ideas during discussion; persistence when explaining a puzzling observation.
slo.keyInquiry: How can we charge conductors? Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 3 to 5 showed that friction and contact transfer electrons, and that contact gives the SAME sign. This lesson answers an open question from Lesson 1: why is a NEUTRAL wall or paper attracted to the balloon, and why is it never repelled? Learners meet induction and earthing, and add them to the model. This prepares for Lesson 7 (distribution of charge) and Lesson 8 (using the electroscope to detect the sign).
slo.safetyNotes: Use only dry, low-voltage materials. No mains electricity. Keep strips and rods away from faces. Handle the gold-leaf electroscope gently because the leaf is fragile and tears easily. Do not let learners touch the cap except when instructed. Keep the room dry: store balloons and strips in a dry place and wipe them before use. A small spark may be felt on touching, which is harmless but should be mentioned beforehand.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Mwangi opens by asking why the neutral wall and paper pieces are attracted to the balloon but never repelled. Learners first predict. They then observe three pieces of evidence: (1) paper pieces and a wall near a negative balloon, (2) a neutral electroscope with a rubbed polythene strip brought near the cap but not touching, where the leaf rises to about 30 degrees and falls back to 0 degrees when the strip is removed, and (3) a four-step induction with earthing in which a finger touch returns the leaf to 0 degrees and the conductor ends with the OPPOSITE sign. In the Explain phase, learners use particle diagrams to show why attraction is stronger than repulsion and contrast contact with induction. They update the Driving Question Board (DQB) and revise their model of the balloon, hair, wall and paper by adding charge separation in the wall and paper.

framework.learnerExperience: Mr Mwangi holds a rubbed balloon (negative) 2 cm above torn paper pieces (about 1 cm x 1 cm). Pieces jump up to the balloon. Learners recall Lesson 1: the unrubbed balloon did nothing. Individually, learners write and sketch a prediction in their notebooks: 'The paper is neutral. It has no charge. So why does it jump to a charged balloon? What do you predict will happen to a neutral electroscope when a negative strip is brought near the cap but NOT touching it?' They draw the leaf at the predicted angle. They also predict: 'If I then touch the cap with my finger while the strip is still near, what will happen to the leaf?' They share with a partner, then write their ideas on sticky notes for the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Wanjiru, Otieno, Amina and Kipchoge all saw the paper jump. Nobody saw it repelled. Let's think about why.' Ask: 'Is the paper charged before the balloon arrives?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds in silence. Cold-call 3 learners (including Amina and Otieno) for their ideas without evaluating them. Say: 'I will not tell you if you are right yet. Draw what you think the electrons in the paper are doing.' Walk around and note common ideas, such as 'the paper must have gained charge' or 'the balloon is sticky'. Remind the class of the Lesson 5 contact result: a conductor touched by a charged object gains the SAME sign. Ask: 'Is the paper touching the balloon when it first jumps?' Record 3 predictions about the electroscope on the board with no judgement.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with individual prediction first: committing to a written prediction creates a cognitive tension that makes learners notice the evidence. Surfacing initial ideas, such as 'paper must be charged', lets the teacher target them in later phases.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check notebooks for: (a) learners who say the paper is already charged, (b) learners who predict the leaf stays at 0 degrees, (c) learners who predict the leaf rises, (d) any learner who mentions electrons moving without contact. Tally on a clipboard how many predicted the leaf would rise (target: identify the groups who need extra support in the Observe phase).

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners rotate through three stations (about 12 minutes each). Station 1, Neutral objects near a charged balloon: A balloon is rubbed on dry hair for 20 strokes (about 10 seconds). Learners hold it about 2 cm above paper pieces, then place it against a painted wall for about 3 minutes (range 2 to 5 minutes) and record what happens. Learners also test an unrubbed balloon (no effect). They record whether the paper is ever repelled before it touches, and what happens to pieces that touch the balloon and fall off. Station 2, Induction on the electroscope: A neutral gold-leaf electroscope has the leaf at 0 degrees. A rubbed polythene strip (negative, rubbed with wool/fur) is brought near the cap WITHOUT touching: the leaf rises to about 30 degrees. The strip is removed: the leaf falls back to 0 degrees. Learners record the angles in a table and answer: 'Did any charge stay on the electroscope?' Station 3, Charging by induction with earthing (Mr Mwangi demonstrates this one while groups watch, then pairs try it in 4 steps): Step 1: Bring the negative strip near the cap, without touching: the leaf rises to about 30 degrees. Step 2: While the strip is still near, touch the cap with a finger (earthing): the leaf falls to 0 degrees. Step 3: Remove the finger FIRST, with the strip still near: the leaf stays at 0 degrees. Step 4: Remove the strip: the leaf rises to about 30 degrees and stays up. Learners record the angle at each step. Sign test: bring the negative strip near again, and the leaf rises further (above 30 degrees), which shows the electroscope is now positively charged. (Learners are told that the leaf rises above 30 degrees when a negative object is brought near an electroscope that is already negative; for a positive electroscope the effect is the opposite, so they compare this with the earlier data and discuss in the Explain phase.) Learners also compare this with Lesson 5, in which touching with the strip left the leaf at about 30 degrees with the SAME sign.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the stations, say: 'Your job is to collect evidence. Write down exactly what you see, with angles in degrees. Do not explain yet.' Model reading the leaf angle against the scale. Circulate and ask each group: 'What happened to the leaf when the strip was brought near but not touching? Where did the strip never touch?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before accepting answers. At Station 3, say: 'Step order matters. The finger comes off BEFORE the strip. Why do you think that is?' Do not answer for them. Ask Kipchoge's group: 'You felt a tiny tingle when your finger touched the cap. What do you think moved?' Remind learners that only electrons move in solids. Cold-call 4 learners across the room to describe one reading each (for example, 'leaf at about 30 degrees with strip near') and record these on the class table. If humidity is a problem, wipe the strip with a dry cloth and remind the class: 'Teachers use dry conditions. Humidity lets charge leak away, as in Mombasa in the rainy season.' Check that learners are only touching the cap when instructed.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table with anomalous-result discussion: recording the same measurements (angles in degrees) at each step lets learners compare induction (no contact, leaf falls back) with induction plus earthing (leaf stays up) and with contact (Lesson 5, same sign). Seeing the numbers side by side makes the pattern visible before any explanation is given. This builds the SEP of analysing and interpreting data.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: learners (a) read the leaf angle within about 5 degrees of 30 degrees and 0 degrees, (b) record all four steps in the correct order, (c) note that the leaf falls to 0 degrees when the strip is removed in Station 2 (no charge left), but stays at about 30 degrees after Step 4 in Station 3 (charge left), (d) say that the strip never touched the cap. Use a checklist with the 4 steps; groups who miss Step 3 are asked to redo it.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of 4 to build explanations from their evidence. Task 1, Charge separation: Using a large sheet, each group draws a particle-level diagram of the neutral electroscope (cap, stem, leaf) as the negative strip is brought near the cap. They show the free electrons in the metal (Lesson 4: conductors have free electrons) being repelled down to the leaf and stem, leaving the cap positive. Both leaf and stem become negative and repel each other, so the leaf rises to about 30 degrees. The total charge is still zero. When the strip is removed, the electrons spread back, and the leaf falls to 0 degrees. Task 2, Earthing and the opposite sign: Groups add the finger step. With the strip near, electrons are repelled through the finger to the Earth. The electroscope now has a deficit of electrons. When the finger is removed and then the strip is removed, the remaining deficit spreads over the cap and leaf, so the leaf rises to about 30 degrees. The electroscope is positive, the OPPOSITE of the strip. They explain why the order (finger off first) matters: otherwise electrons flow back from the Earth. Task 3, Contrast with contact: Groups complete a two-column comparison of contact (Lesson 5: same sign, strip touches) and induction (opposite sign, strip never touches, earthing needed). Task 4, Back to the phenomenon: Groups apply the idea to the wall and paper. The negative balloon repels electrons in the neutral paper, so electrons shift slightly away, leaving the near side positive and the far side negative. The nearer positive side is attracted more strongly than the farther negative side is repelled, so there is a net attraction. In an insulator such as paper or a painted wall, the electrons shift only slightly within their atoms, but the effect is the same. This is why the balloon sticks to the wall and the paper jumps, and why a neutral object is attracted but never repelled. Pieces that touch the balloon may gain a little electrons and the same sign, and then fall off. They finish with: 'Where do the charges in the paper come from?' (They were there all along; they just moved a little. No charge was created.)
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use only electrons as the movers. Protons stay in the nucleus. Never write that positive charge moved.' Circulate and ask: 'Where did the electrons in the electroscope go when I touched the cap?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to explain Task 2 using their diagrams. Probe: 'If the electrons left, why is the electroscope positive and not neutral?' Prompt for the term 'deficit of electrons'. Ask Amina's group: 'Does induction explain why the balloon is attracted to the wall in Mombasa on a rainy day?' Guide them to the humidity idea: water vapour lets charge leak away from the balloon, so there is less to induce. Ask: 'Why is a neutral object attracted but never repelled?' and wait for answers about the nearer charge. Correct misconceptions directly: 'The paper does not become permanently charged by induction. It only separates charge.' Use the phrase 'Induction gives the OPPOSITE sign. Contact gives the SAME sign.' and have the class repeat it. Select 2 groups to present diagrams, then ask the class to critique them using the evidence ('Which data supports this?').
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model-based reasoning with Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER): learners build a particle-level model of electron movement and use their angle data as evidence to justify claims about the sign of charge. Comparing contact and induction in a two-column table helps them to separate two ideas that are easily confused. Applying the model to the paper and wall transfers the idea back to the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators of understanding: (a) diagrams show electrons, not protons, moving; (b) the near side of the paper is labelled positive and the far side negative; (c) learners state that the electroscope ends positive after induction with earthing; (d) learners say that attraction is stronger because the opposite charge is closer; (e) learners correctly say contact gives the same sign and induction the opposite. Use a 3-question exit check: 'What sign does the electroscope have after Step 4? Why was the finger removed first? Why is paper attracted but not repelled?' Learners who say the paper is 'charged' or that protons move are given a short follow-up conversation.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class DQB from Lesson 1. In groups, they review the questions on it and the sticky notes from today's Predict phase. They (1) move or mark questions now answered, for example 'Why is paper attracted to the balloon if it is neutral?' and 'Why does the balloon stick to the wall?'; (2) write the answer on a new card with the evidence (angles of 30 degrees and 0 degrees; the 4 steps); and (3) add new questions that arise, such as 'Why does the electroscope leaf rise above 30 degrees when a negative strip is brought near?', 'How do we know the sign of a charge?', 'Does charge spread out evenly on a conductor?', 'Why does the shock from a woollen jersey happen?' and 'Is the shock like lightning, as Kipchoge asked?'. Each group places at least one new question on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which questions can we now answer with evidence from today?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to read a question and say whether it is answered, partly answered or still open. Ask Otieno to link his observation of the balloon on the classroom wall to today's explanation. Ask Kipchoge to restate his question about lightning and say: 'We will return to this in Lesson 7 when we look at where charge goes on a conductor and sharp points.' Group the new questions under the KICD inquiry questions (for example 'How can we detect and measure electric charge?'). Ensure each answered question has evidence on its card, not just an opinion.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding: separating answered, partly answered and open questions shows learners that science is cumulative and that each lesson links to the next. Writing evidence on each answer card reinforces evidence-based reasoning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: learners' answer cards cite specific data (for example 'leaf stays at about 30 degrees after removing the strip'); new questions are testable and connected to charge sign, distribution or discharge; at least 80% of groups add one new question. Note which questions are most common to guide Lessons 7 and 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out their model from Lesson 5: a labelled particle-level diagram of the balloon, hair, wall and paper. Individually, they revise it by (1) showing the neutral wall and paper near the negative balloon with electrons shifted away, so the near surface is positive and the far side negative; (2) adding arrows for the electrostatic force: a stronger attraction between the balloon and the nearer positive charges, and a weaker repulsion from the farther negative charges; (3) labelling that no charge was created and total charge is conserved; (4) adding a note on the effect of humidity: water vapour lets charge leak away, so the balloon falls quickly in Mombasa. They also add a small inset showing the electroscope with induction and earthing (4 steps), and write 2 to 3 sentences answering: 'Why is neutral paper attracted to the balloon but never repelled?' They colour-code electrons and use a different colour for the changes made today. Finally, they note one thing their model still cannot explain, such as the spark from a woollen jersey in Nairobi.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your model must now explain the wall and the paper. Show me electrons, not protons, moving.' Circulate and ask: 'Where are the electrons in the paper now? Why is the near side positive?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to explain one change they made. Prompt struggling learners: 'Is the paper charged overall, or just separated?' Ask the class: 'What is the difference between charge separation and gaining charge?' Check that all models show a balloon with an excess of electrons (negative) and hair with a deficit (positive), as in earlier lessons. Collect models for review. Preview Lesson 7: 'Next, we ask where the charge goes on a conductor. Could that help explain the shock Wanjiru and Kipchoge felt?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision (SEP 2: developing and using models): revising the same particle-level diagram each lesson shows how new evidence refines explanations. Adding induction to the model links charge separation to the anchoring phenomenon. Noting what the model cannot yet explain builds metacognition and motivates the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators on the revised model: (a) electrons shifted away from the balloon in the wall and paper; (b) near side positive and far side negative, with the near attraction larger; (c) no protons moving; (d) a statement that charge is conserved; (e) humidity noted as a cause of leakage; (f) one unanswered question listed. Use a 4-point checklist; learners who miss (a) or (c) are revisited at the start of Lesson 7.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did learners clearly separate induction (opposite sign, earthing needed, no touching) from contact (same sign) in Lesson 5? Which diagrams still show protons moving? (2) Did the step order with the finger (remove finger before the strip) cause confusion? If so, plan a short re-demonstration. (3) Did dry conditions hold? Note any groups whose leaf did not rise to about 30 degrees and check the strips, cloth and room humidity. (4) Were learners able to apply the idea to the neutral paper and wall, and not just the electroscope? (5) Which learners (for example Amina with the humidity idea and Kipchoge with the lightning idea) need to be heard more? (6) Which new DQB questions should shape Lesson 7?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: A neutral electroscope with a negative polythene strip brought near the cap, not touching: the leaf rose to about 30 degrees and fell back to 0 degrees when the strip was removed. With the strip near and a finger touching the cap (earthing), the leaf fell to 0 degrees. After removing the finger and then the strip, the leaf rose to about 30 degrees and stayed up. Neutral paper pieces jumped to the negative balloon and the balloon stuck to the wall, with no repulsion seen.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: A charged object can separate charge in a neutral object without touching it (induction). Earthing lets electrons flow to or from the Earth, and charging by induction with earthing gives the OPPOSITE sign, while contact gives the SAME sign. Only electrons move, and charge is not created but transferred.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The negative balloon repels electrons in the neutral paper and wall, leaving the near surface positive and the far side negative. The nearer positive charge is attracted more strongly than the farther negative charge is repelled, so a neutral object is attracted but never repelled. This explains why the paper jumps and the balloon sticks to the wall. On humid days, such as in Mombasa, the balloon's charge leaks away, so the effect is weak or short-lived.

LESSONS.title: Distribution of Charge on Conductors: Outer Surfaces, Points, Sparks and Lightning Conductors
LESSONS.aresKeywords: charge distribution, outer surface, proof plane, point discharge, spark, lightning conductor, earthing, electroscope, leaf divergence

slo.purpose: Learners investigate where charge sits on a charged conductor, and use point discharge to explain sparks such as the Nairobi jersey shock and the action of lightning conductors. This moves the class closer to answering: Where do electric charges come from, and why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects?
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to state that (1) charge on a conductor collects on the outer surface (hollow can: outside about 40 degrees, inside 0 degrees), (2) charge is concentrated at points (pointed end about 45 degrees, flat end about 20 degrees), and (3) point discharge, in which a strong field at a point ionises the air and charge leaks away, explains sparks and lightning conductors.
slo.skills: Planning and carrying out investigations (using a proof plane and electroscope); analysing and interpreting data (comparing leaf divergence in degrees); constructing explanations (claim-evidence-reasoning); developing and using models (revising the particle-level diagram); communication and collaboration.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about invisible forces, respect for evidence, care and safety when handling charged apparatus, and appreciation of how science protects buildings and people in lightning-prone areas such as Kericho and Kisumu.
slo.keyInquiry: Where does charge go on a conductor? (KICD Key Inquiry Question 5), linked to the driving question: Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 4 showed that conductors have free electrons that move through the material, and Lesson 5 showed that a conductor touched by a charged object gains the same sign of charge by electron transfer. Lesson 6 introduced earthing. Lesson 7 asks where the transferred electrons end up on a conductor, and how this explains the spark Kipchoge asked about (Is the shock like lightning?). It prepares Lesson 8 (detecting and measuring charge with the electroscope) and Lesson 9 (applications, including lightning conductors).
slo.safetyNotes: Mr Mwangi uses only dry apparatus in a dry room and does all charging himself (small charges of about nC only). Learners must never touch a real lightning conductor or go near one in a storm, and should shelter indoors during thunderstorms, away from open fields, trees and Lake Victoria shores. Handle the fragile gold leaf gently, and keep pointed metal away from faces and eyes. Do not run sparking demonstrations near flammable materials or fuel.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Mwangi begins with Kipchoge's question from the Nairobi dry-season day: is the jersey shock like lightning? Learners predict where the extra electrons will sit on a charged metal can and on a pear-shaped conductor. They then use a proof plane and a gold-leaf electroscope to collect data: outside of the can gives about 40 degrees and inside gives 0 degrees, while the pointed end gives about 45 degrees and the flat end about 20 degrees. They explain the pattern with repulsion between mobile electrons (from Lessons 4 and 5), use point discharge to explain sparks and lightning conductors in Kericho and Kisumu, and revise the DQB and their particle-level models of the balloon, hair, wall and paper to include charge spreading out and leaking from points.

framework.learnerExperience: Wanjiru recalls how her hair stands up after combing on dry Nairobi mornings, and Kipchoge asks, Is the shock from a woollen jersey like lightning? Learners look at a hollow metal can on an insulating stand and a pear-shaped metal conductor. Individually, then in pairs, they draw each object and use dots (for extra electrons) to predict where the extra electrons will sit if each conductor is given a negative charge from a rubbed polythene strip. They also predict which spot will make an electroscope leaf rise higher when touched with a proof plane: outside or inside the can, and the pointed end or the flat end. Each pair writes a one-sentence reason using what they know about free electrons in conductors and like charges repelling.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Kipchoge asked whether our jersey shock is like lightning. Today we find out where charge goes when it sits on a metal object.' Show the can and the pear-shaped conductor. Say: 'Draw the object. Put dots where you think the extra electrons will be. Write why.' Give 2 minutes of silent individual drawing. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after asking, 'Where would 10 electrons push each other to, if they can move freely?' Cold-call 4 learners to share predictions without saying whether they are right. Record the predictions in tally form on the board (outside, inside, spread evenly, at points). Ask Amina, Otieno and Wanjiru to explain their reasoning to the class. Say: 'We will test every prediction with data. Keep your drawing; we will revise it.' Do not give the answer yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with a individual-to-pair drawing task: committing to a prediction and reasoning before evidence makes later conflict between the prediction and the data visible, which drives conceptual change. Learners reuse the Lesson 4 and 5 idea of free electrons in conductors.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the drawings: (1) Do learners draw dots as electrons (negative), not as positive charges moving? (2) Does the reasoning mention that electrons are free to move and repel each other? (3) Tally the number of learners predicting outside, inside, even and points. Look for the misconception that charge spreads evenly through the inside of the metal, and note which learners use words such as 'repel' or 'spread out'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners watch Mr Mwangi's demonstration in dry conditions and, in groups of 4, record and compare data. Part A: The hollow metal can is charged negatively using a rubbed polythene strip (contact charging, Lesson 5). A proof plane is touched on the OUTSIDE of the can, then touched to the cap of the gold-leaf electroscope; the leaf rises to about 40 degrees. The electroscope is discharged by earthing with a finger (Lesson 6), returning the leaf to 0 degrees. The proof plane is then touched on the INSIDE of the same can and transferred to the electroscope; the leaf stays at 0 degrees. Part B: The pear-shaped (pointed) conductor is charged. The proof plane touched at the pointed end gives about 45 degrees; after earthing the electroscope to 0 degrees, the flat end gives about 20 degrees. Part C: The class discusses the Nairobi spark: what happens to the crackle in a dark room after removing a woollen jersey? Groups record a data table: location, leaf angle (degrees), and a sketch of where the charge is. Groups explain why the inside reading is 0 degrees even though the can is charged.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Watch the leaf, not my hands. Record the angle in degrees.' Before each touch, ask: 'What do you predict for this reading?' Make learners say a number or a range. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after each reading before anyone speaks. Ask: 'What changed between outside and inside?' Cold-call 3 groups for each part. Ensure the electroscope is earthed to 0 degrees before each new reading: 'Why must I touch the cap with my finger before the next test?' (Lesson 6 earthing). Draw the results table on the board and fill it in as: outside 40, inside 0, pointed end 45, flat end 20. Say: 'A proof plane picks up a small sample of charge from the spot it touches. A higher leaf angle means more charge at that spot.' Circulate and ask: 'Is it that the inside has no electrons, or that the extra electrons are not there?' Ask learners to link 'a rubbed balloon gains about 1 nC' to the idea that charge also sits on surfaces. Remind groups that the metal can is a conductor, unlike the balloon (an insulator), so its charge can move.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table and pattern-finding with a gallery of numbers: comparing leaf angles across locations (40 vs 0, 45 vs 20) lets learners see a clear pattern through quantitative evidence. Using a proof plane as a probe shows an invisible quantity by a visible measure (leaf divergence in degrees).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Learners correctly record 40 and 0 degrees (outside and inside), and 45 and 20 degrees (pointed and flat ends) with units. (2) Learners state that a bigger leaf angle means more charge was collected. (3) Learners remember to earth the electroscope between tests. (4) In their explanations, learners connect inside = 0 degrees to 'no charge on the inside surface', not 'no electrons inside the metal'. Note any group that claims the can is not charged because the inside reads 0.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups, learners write a claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) explanation answering: 'Where does charge go on a conductor, and why?' Claim: charge collects on the outer surface and is most concentrated at points. Evidence: outside 40 degrees vs inside 0 degrees; pointed end 45 degrees vs flat end 20 degrees. Reasoning: the free electrons in a conductor repel each other (like charges repel), so they move as far apart as possible, to the outer surface; at a sharply curved point they crowd more closely together. Then learners apply point discharge: at a point, the strong electric field ionises the air nearby, and charge leaks away into the air. They use this to explain (a) the Nairobi spark and faint crackle from a woollen jersey or comb on a dry day, and (b) lightning conductors on buildings in Kericho (tea country, frequent lightning) and Kisumu: a pointed metal rod on top of a building joined by thick copper strip to a buried earth plate. The pointed rod lets charge leak away gradually, and if lightning strikes it gives a safe path to the ground (earthing) instead of through the building. Learners compare a lightning conductor with Kipchoge's question: is the jersey shock like lightning? They explain that both are discharges, with lightning a much larger one.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use your numbers. A claim without evidence is just an opinion.' Provide CER sentence starters on the board. Ask: 'Why do free electrons end up on the outside?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to complete the sentence 'The electrons repel each other so...'. Ask: 'Why would a point have more charge crowded together than a flat end?' Accept answers using the data and gently correct statements such as 'positive charges moved' (in solids only electrons move). Introduce the term 'point discharge': 'At a sharp point the field is so strong that it can ionise the air, and charge leaks away.' Show a picture or model of a lightning conductor in Kericho: pointed rod, thick copper strip, buried earth plate. Ask: 'Why a pointed rod and not a flat plate? Why thick copper? Why buried in the ground?' (point discharge, copper is a conductor, earthing from Lesson 6). Ask Kipchoge: 'Is the jersey shock like lightning?' Give the idea that both are discharges, differing in size. Do not use 'static electricity' as an explanation; use 'electrostatic force' and 'discharge'. Hold a quick exit-check: 'Write one sentence linking the pointed end reading of 45 degrees to a lightning conductor.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with transfer: connecting numerical evidence to a particle-level reason (electron repulsion) and then applying it to an unfamiliar real context (lightning conductors in Kericho, Kisumu) shows whether learners can use the idea rather than only recall it.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) claims that use 'outer surface' and 'points'; (2) evidence quoting both readings with degrees; (3) reasoning that includes repulsion between electrons and free movement in conductors; (4) correct use of 'discharge' and 'earthing'; (5) transfer: learners explain that the pointed rod leaks charge and the copper strip and earth plate carry the charge safely to the ground. Misconceptions to watch for: 'lightning conductors attract lightning', 'charge is created at the point', or 'positive charge flows through the copper'. Correct with 'electrons move, charge is transferred, not created'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB. They review which questions are answered by today's evidence: KICD question 5 (Where does charge go on a conductor?) and part of question 7 (How is electrostatics used in everyday life?). They add new questions on sticky notes, for example: 'Why does charge stay on the balloon but spread out on metal?', 'Can a lightning conductor stop lightning?', 'Why do fuel tankers trail a chain?', 'How does the electroscope tell us the sign of charge?' Learners place each note on the board under a category (answered, partly answered, new question) and write the evidence that answers it (e.g., outside 40 degrees, inside 0 degrees; pointed end 45 degrees, flat end 20 degrees). Amina asks whether humid coastal weather in Mombasa changes point discharge; this is added as a new question.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Which of our questions can we now answer with evidence? Move the sticky note and write the evidence on it.' Ask 3 learners (cold-call) to move a note and justify it. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before asking for new questions: 'What does today's evidence make you wonder next?' Collect at least 5 new questions. Point out that Lesson 8 will answer 'How can we detect and measure electric charge?' and Lesson 9 will answer 'How is electrostatics used in everyday life?' Praise questions that start with 'why' or 'how' and are testable. Link Amina's question back to humidity: 'Remember that on humid days water vapour lets charge escape; how might this connect to point discharge?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a living record: moving questions to 'answered' with evidence helps learners see their own progress, and new questions keep the inquiry student-driven and coherent across lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that notes are moved only with evidence (e.g., quoting 40 and 0 degrees, or 45 and 20 degrees). Count how many new questions are testable and linked to the phenomenon. Look for learners who connect Amina's humidity idea or Kipchoge's lightning question to today's data. Note learners who give no new question and follow up individually.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise their labelled particle-level diagram of the balloon, hair, wall and paper. In the previous lessons they showed electrons transferred from hair (positive) to balloon (negative), and induced separation of charge in the neutral wall and paper. Now they add: (1) the extra electrons on a charged conductor (such as a metal object touched by the balloon) are drawn spread on the outer surface, with closer spacing at any pointed part; (2) a note that on the insulating balloon the charge stays where it was rubbed, unlike on a metal conductor where it moves; (3) a small inset sketch of point discharge: electrons leaking from a point into the air, linked to the Nairobi spark and faint crackle from a woollen jersey, and to the lightning conductor in Kericho. They label the leaf angles (40 and 0 degrees; 45 and 20 degrees) beside the inset as evidence and write a two-sentence caption. They compare models with a partner and add one revision in a different colour.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add what is new in a different colour. Label everything. Use the word electrons for what moves.' Remind learners that the balloon is negative and hair is positive in every diagram. Circulate and ask: 'Where is the charge on the metal object in your model? Why there?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to explain their revision. Ask: 'What does your model now explain that it could not explain before?' and 'What can it still not explain?' Collect the answers (for example, how to measure the amount of charge, which is Lesson 8) and add them to the DQB. Tell learners to keep the models for Lesson 8.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Iterative model revision: adding new particle-level features each lesson, with colour-coded changes, shows how evidence changes explanation, and identifying the model's limits creates purpose for the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check models for: (1) electrons (not positive charges) shown on the outer surface of a conductor; (2) closer spacing at a point; (3) a point discharge inset with electrons leaking into air; (4) correct signs (balloon negative, hair positive); (5) evidence labels of 40, 0, 45 and 20 degrees; (6) a stated limitation of the model. Revisit learners whose models show charge inside the metal or evenly spread, and ask them to point to the data that disagrees.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners explain the 0 degrees inside reading as 'no charge on the inside' rather than 'no electrons in the metal'? (2) How many learners used electron repulsion in their reasoning, and who still thought charge spreads evenly? (3) Did the dry conditions give clear readings of about 40, 0, 45 and 20 degrees, and did I remember to earth the electroscope between tests? (4) Did any learners say 'positive charge moved' or 'static electricity' as an explanation, and how did I respond? (5) Could learners connect the pointed end reading to the lightning conductors in Kericho and Kisumu and to Kipchoge's jersey shock question? (6) Which questions on the DQB still need evidence for Lesson 8 (detecting and measuring charge) and Lesson 9 (applications)? Plan follow-up for learners who need to rehearse the CER structure.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that a charged hollow metal can gave an electroscope leaf reading of about 40 degrees when the proof plane touched the outside and 0 degrees when it touched the inside. On the pear-shaped conductor, the pointed end gave about 45 degrees and the flat end about 20 degrees.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that the free electrons on a charged conductor repel each other and move to the outer surface, and that charge is most concentrated at points. At a point, the strong field ionises the air and charge leaks away (point discharge), while earthing lets charge flow safely to the ground.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: This explains why a woollen jersey shock in dry Nairobi is a small spark (a discharge) and why lightning conductors, with a pointed rod joined by thick copper strip to a buried earth plate, protect buildings in Kericho and Kisumu. It also adds to our model of how electrons, not created charge, move and build up around the balloon, hair, wall and paper.
