LESSONS.title: Detecting and Measuring Charge: The Gold-Leaf Electroscope
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one double period of 80 minutes if the practical is done in groups)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: gold-leaf electroscope, leaf divergence, detect charge, sign of charge, discharge, earthing, amount of charge

slo.purpose: To let learners use a gold-leaf electroscope to detect charge, find its sign, discharge it, and relate leaf divergence to the amount of charge, so they can answer how we know that the balloon is charged and how much.
slo.knowledge: Learners explain that a gold-leaf electroscope detects charge because charge on the cap and leaf makes the leaf and stem repel (like charges repel). A larger leaf divergence means more charge (20 strokes gives about 30 degrees; 40 strokes gives about 50 degrees). A charged electroscope is used to find the sign of an unknown charge: an increase in divergence means the same sign, and a decrease means the opposite sign. Touching the cap with a finger (earthing) lets electrons flow to or from the Earth and returns the leaf to 0 degrees.
slo.skills: Developing and using models; planning and carrying out investigations; analysing and interpreting data (leaf divergence in degrees); constructing explanations using evidence; communicating scientific ideas clearly.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about invisible forces; honesty in recording readings; careful teamwork and safe handling of apparatus; respect for evidence when it contradicts a prediction.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD Key Inquiry Question 6: How can we detect and measure electric charge? This also advances the Driving Question: Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 5, 6 and 7 showed how charge is moved onto conductors by contact, by induction and by earthing, and where it sits on a conductor. In Lesson 8 learners turn the electroscope from something they have used into a measuring tool. They gather evidence that the balloon really carries charge, that its sign can be tested, and that more rubbing gives more charge. This evidence feeds the final model in Lesson 9.
slo.safetyNotes: Gold leaf is very thin and tears easily, so handle it only with the teacher's guidance and keep the electroscope case closed or away from draughts. Use only dry polythene strips, wool/fur and perspex rods. Keep the apparatus away from sinks and open windows because humidity makes charge leak away. Do not touch the cap during the readings. Nothing in this lesson uses mains electricity. Any spark felt is tiny and harmless, but learners should not rub and then touch each other's faces.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Mwangi opens with Amina's claim that the balloon 'never works' at her coastal home in Mombasa, and Wanjiru's feeling of a shock after combing her hair. He asks, 'How could we tell, without relying on feelings, whether something is charged, and by how much?' Learners predict what a gold-leaf electroscope will do when a rubbed polythene strip is brought near the cap. In groups they then observe: a neutral electroscope with the leaf at 0 degrees; the leaf rising to about 30 degrees when a negative strip (20 strokes) is brought near without touching; the leaf staying at about 30 degrees after the strip touches the cap and is removed; the leaf rising to about 50 degrees with a stronger charge (40 strokes); the sign test, where a negative object raises the leaf above 30 degrees and a positive object lowers it below 30 degrees; and finger earthing returning the leaf to 0 degrees. In the Explain phase, learners use particle-level reasoning, with electrons only moving, to explain each result. They then add new questions to the Driving Question Board and revise their model of the balloon, hair, wall and paper by adding a 'how do we know?' detector box showing that the balloon's charge can be detected and compared.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in groups of four around one gold-leaf electroscope on a desk. They recall Wanjiru's hair standing up and Amina's balloon failing in Mombasa. Each learner draws a neutral electroscope (cap, stem, leaf) and predicts, with a sketch, what the leaf will do when a rubbed polythene strip (20 strokes with wool) is brought near the cap without touching it. They also predict what happens if the strip is rubbed with 40 strokes instead. Then they predict what will happen when the cap is touched with a finger. They write a prediction with a reason using the words 'electrons', 'repel' and 'leaf'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last lesson we saw that charge crowds at points. Today's question: how can we detect charge and measure it, since we cannot see electrons?' Hold up the electroscope and point out the cap, metal stem and leaf. Show the leaf hanging down at 0 degrees. Say: 'Draw this neutral electroscope, then predict. Do not touch anything yet.' Give 2 minutes of silent individual writing. WAIT TIME: after asking 'What do you think the leaf will do when the negative strip comes near the cap?' wait 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 3 learners, including one from a group that has not yet spoken, and ask each, 'What is your reason?' Record the three predictions on the board without judging them. Ask Amina to say how she would know whether her balloon in Mombasa was charged at all.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with individual sketches: committing to a prediction and a reason before seeing data makes learners aware of what they already think about charge and electron movement, so the later observations either support or challenge those ideas. Learners' ideas are compared with the evidence in the Explain phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the sketches for these indicators: (1) the leaf drawn as lifting away from the stem; (2) the word 'repel' or 'same charge' used in the reason; (3) any mention of electrons moving onto or off the cap. Tally on the board how many learners predict 'leaf rises' versus 'no change'. Note who predicts that 40 strokes gives a bigger angle than 20 strokes. Note common ideas, such as 'the leaf is attracted to the strip', to revisit in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of four with an electroscope, a polythene strip, wool/fur, a perspex rod, silk and a protractor or angle scale card placed behind the leaf. Step 1: Record the neutral leaf angle (0 degrees). Step 2: Rub the polythene strip with wool 20 strokes, bring it near the cap without touching it, and record the angle (about 30 degrees). Remove the strip and record what happens to the leaf. Step 3: Touch the strip to the cap (contact), remove the strip and record the angle (stays at about 30 degrees). Step 4: Sign test. With the electroscope now charged negatively at about 30 degrees, bring a second rubbed polythene strip (negative) near the cap and record the angle (rises above 30 degrees). Then bring a rubbed perspex rod (positive, rubbed with silk) near the cap and record the angle (falls below 30 degrees). Step 5: Earth the electroscope by touching the cap with a finger and record the angle (0 degrees). Step 6: Repeat the contact charging with 40 strokes and record the angle (about 50 degrees). Learners fill in a results table: Action, Number of strokes, Leaf divergence (degrees), Observation. They also watch a short teacher demonstration of the balloon (rubbed 20 strokes) brought near the cap, which makes the leaf rise, showing that the balloon from the phenomenon is charged.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the apparatus and say: 'Handle the leaf gently. Take readings from the scale behind the leaf at eye level and do not touch the cap unless the instructions say so.' Move around the groups and ask: 'What happened to the leaf when the strip came near, and what happened when you took the strip away?' Ask each group to read out one measurement. Use cold-call: select 4 groups and ask each for the angle for one step, then compare their readings on the board (about 0, 30, 30, above 30, below 30, 0, 50). Prompt: 'Why do you think the angle is bigger with 40 strokes?' but do not give the answer yet. WAIT TIME: after the sign test say, 'Look at your table. What pattern do you see?' and wait 10-15 seconds in silence. Remind groups to keep the demonstration dry and to keep their hands away from the cap. Do the balloon demonstration at the front: rub the balloon 20 strokes on dry hair, hold it near the cap and show the leaf rising.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table with structured observation: recording angles in degrees for each action turns what learners see into comparable evidence. Comparing readings across groups shows which results are consistent (about 0, 30 and 50 degrees) and helps them see the pattern before an explanation is given.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) angles recorded within about 5 degrees of 0, 30 and 50 for the corresponding steps; (2) the sign test recorded correctly, with an angle above 30 for negative and below 30 for positive; (3) learners reading the scale at eye level; (4) earthing recorded as returning the leaf to 0 degrees. Use a quick tally of groups with correct results, and help groups whose strips were damp or rubbed too few times.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups use their results table to explain each result in terms of electrons. First they draw a particle-level diagram of the electroscope when the negative strip is near the cap: electrons in the metal are pushed down the stem to the leaf, so leaf and stem both have excess electrons and repel. They then explain contact: electrons move from the strip to the electroscope, so the leaf stays up at about 30 degrees even after the strip is removed (same sign as the strip). For the sign test they reason that adding more negative charge pushes more electrons into the leaf and stem, so repulsion and the angle increase; a positive rod attracts electrons up toward the cap, so the leaf and stem have fewer excess electrons and the angle falls. For earthing, they explain that electrons flow from the electroscope to the Earth through the finger, leaving the electroscope neutral at 0 degrees. They compare 20 strokes (about 30 degrees) with 40 strokes (about 50 degrees) and write a statement: 'More charge on the leaf and stem gives more repulsion and a bigger leaf divergence.' They finish by relating this to the balloon: the rubbed balloon (negative, about 1 nC) caused the leaf to rise because it carries excess electrons.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use only electrons for movers. Protons stay in the nucleus.' Ask, 'Where did the electrons in the leaf come from when the strip touched the cap?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before calling on anyone. Cold-call 3 learners to explain one step each, then ask a fourth to challenge or add to the explanation. Correct 'the leaf is attracted to the strip' by asking, 'If the strip is removed and the leaf stays up, can the strip be the thing pulling it?' Ask, 'Why does a positive rod make the leaf fall, not rise? What is it doing to the electrons?' Point out that a leaf that rises only shows the object is charged and not the sign; a rise on an already charged electroscope shows the same sign, a fall shows the opposite sign. Note that a neutral object can attract by induction, so repulsion (a rise) is the sure test. Ask Kipchoge to explain how the leaf's behaviour is like a small version of the spark he asked about. Summarise: 'Leaf divergence tells us the amount of charge, and the sign test tells us the sign.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with particle-level drawings: each group states a claim (for example, 'The electroscope now has excess electrons'), cites evidence from their table (for example, 'the leaf stayed at about 30 degrees after the strip was removed'), and gives reasoning using electron movement and like charges repelling. This links the measurements to the model and prevents memorising rules without understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for: (1) 'electrons move' rather than 'positive charge moves'; (2) the statement 'like charges repel' used to explain the leaf rising; (3) the sign test explained as an increase for the same sign and a decrease for the opposite sign; (4) earthing explained as electrons flowing to the Earth; (5) a link between bigger angle and more charge (50 degrees against 30 degrees). Use a 3-question exit check on mini whiteboards: 'What does a bigger angle show?', 'What does a decrease in angle show?', 'What does earthing do?' Count correct whiteboards and revisit the sign test if fewer than most are correct.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board and look at the questions from earlier lessons. Each learner writes one new question or answer on a sticky note. Possible new questions: 'How can we measure charge in coulombs and not only in degrees?', 'Why did the balloon stick for less time in Mombasa?', 'Can an electroscope detect charge from a lightning storm in Kisumu?', 'Why does the leaf slowly fall on a humid day?' Groups move sticky notes that have been answered (for example, 'How can we detect and measure electric charge?') to the 'Answered' section with a short evidence statement, such as 'The leaf rose to about 30 degrees with 20 strokes and about 50 degrees with 40 strokes.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which questions can we now answer with our electroscope evidence?' Give 2 minutes for writing, then WAIT TIME: ask 'Which question should we move first and why?' and wait 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to place a note and justify it using data. Ask Amina to restate her Mombasa question and ask the class how an electroscope could help test the humidity idea (the leaf would fall back to 0 degrees faster). Keep questions about applications, such as Kericho lightning conductors and fuel tankers in Nairobi, for Lesson 9.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with evidence-based question sorting: asking learners to justify moving a question to 'Answered' using measurements keeps the focus on evidence and shows how the unit's questions are being resolved step by step. New questions keep learner curiosity driving the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each sticky note is a testable or clear question, that moved notes include a data-based justification (angle in degrees), and that at least a few new questions link detection to the balloon, humidity or lightning. Note which learners ask only recall questions and prompt them with 'What would you change to test it?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise their labelled particle-level diagram of the balloon, hair, wall and paper from earlier lessons. They add a new 'How do we know?' box showing a gold-leaf electroscope near the negative balloon, with electrons drawn moving down to the leaf and stem and the leaf at about 30 degrees. They add arrows for the electrostatic force between leaf and stem, a note that 40 strokes (more electrons transferred) would raise the leaf to about 50 degrees, and an earthing path showing electrons flowing through a finger to the Earth. They keep the labels: balloon negative, hair positive, wall and paper neutral. Each learner writes two sentences under the model: one on how we detect charge and one on how we know its sign.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add the new box to your model. Use arrows for electron movement and label every angle in degrees.' Circulate and ask, 'Where are the extra electrons in your diagram, and what is the leaf doing because of them?' WAIT TIME: ask 'What would your model show if the balloon were rubbed more?' and wait 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to share one change to their model. Remind learners that charge is not created: electrons are transferred and total charge is conserved. Check that no diagram shows protons moving. Ask them to keep the model for Lesson 9, when they will write the final full explanation.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Iterative model revision: adding the electroscope detector to the existing particle-level model connects measurable evidence (degrees) to the invisible electron transfer. Revising the same model across lessons shows how ideas build and become more complete.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a checklist: (1) electrons shown in the leaf and stem with correct sign; (2) leaf angle labelled in degrees with 30 and 50 linked to the number of strokes; (3) earthing shown as electron flow to the Earth; (4) balloon negative, hair positive, and wall and paper neutral still labelled correctly; (5) a sentence that links larger divergence to more charge. Ask learners who miss an item to add it before the end of the lesson.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Did most groups obtain readings close to 0, 30 and 50 degrees, and if not, was dampness or too few strokes the cause? Did learners keep to electrons as the only movers in the Explain phase? Which learners confused 'attraction' with 'detection' of charge and thought the leaf was pulled to the strip? Did the sign test make sense to learners, especially why a rise is a surer test than attraction? What did Amina's Mombasa question show about the class's understanding of humidity? Plan to use the evidence from this lesson, especially the sign test, earthing and the relationship between strokes and angle, as the starting point for Lesson 9's applications and final explanation.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Record what you observed with the gold-leaf electroscope: the leaf at 0 degrees when neutral; about 30 degrees with a negative polythene strip (20 strokes); the leaf staying up after contact; about 50 degrees with 40 strokes; the angle going above 30 degrees with a negative object and below 30 degrees with a positive object; and 0 degrees after earthing with a finger.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Write what you learned: a gold-leaf electroscope detects charge because the leaf and stem carry the same sign and repel; a bigger leaf divergence shows more charge; an increase on a charged electroscope shows the same sign and a decrease shows the opposite sign; earthing lets electrons flow to or from the Earth and discharges the electroscope.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Explain how this helps answer the Driving Question: the rubbed balloon is shown to be charged because it makes the leaf diverge, its negative sign can be tested, and the amount of charge relates to the number of strokes because more electrons are transferred, not created.

LESSONS.title: Applications and Consolidation: From the Mysterious Balloon to Lightning Conductors, and the Final Explanation
LESSONS.aresKeywords: lightning conductor, point discharge, earthing, fuel tanker bonding, photocopier, electrostatic precipitator, final explanation, transfer of electrons, conservation of charge

slo.purpose: Learners apply the ideas from Lessons 1 to 8 to explain how electrostatics is used and managed in technology, and then write a complete final explanation of the anchoring phenomenon (the rubbed balloon, hair, wall and paper) that answers the main driving question.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson learners should be able to: (1) explain how a lightning conductor protects a building in Kericho or Kisumu using point discharge and earthing; (2) explain why a fuel tanker at a Nairobi petrol depot trails an earthing chain or bonding wire; (3) describe how a photocopier and an electrostatic precipitator (e.g. at Athi River cement factory) use attraction between unlike charges; (4) write a final explanation of the balloon phenomenon covering friction, transfer of electrons, signs of charge, hair repulsion, induction on the wall and paper, humidity, the 1 nC charge value and conservation of charge.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (revising the particle-level model of balloon, hair, wall and paper); constructing explanations; analysing and interpreting data (humidity data, 1 nC balloon charge, electroscope and distribution readings); obtaining, evaluating and communicating information; transferring ideas to new situations.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about how the invisible forces around us are used and controlled; respect for safety in storms and near fuel; appreciation of the value of evidence; collaboration and open-mindedness when revising ideas; pride in Kenyan engineers and technology.
slo.keyInquiry: Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects? (Also: How is electrostatics used in everyday life?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson of the storyline. Lessons 1 to 8 gave learners the pieces: charge signs and the rule for attraction and repulsion (L2), friction and electron transfer (L3), conductors and insulators (L4), contact charging (L5), induction and earthing (L6), charge on outer surfaces and point discharge (L7), and detecting charge with the electroscope (L8). Here learners use L7 point discharge and L6 earthing to understand technology, then bring everything together, complete the DQB, compare their Lesson 1 model with their final model, and write the final explanation of the anchoring phenomenon.
slo.safetyNotes: Mr Mwangi uses only dry, low-energy demonstrations with the balloon, polythene strip and electroscope. No high voltage equipment is used; applications are studied through diagrams, short video or images and role-play. Remind learners never to shelter under a lone tree or stand in open ground during a thunderstorm, and never to use phones near fuel or take part in fuel handling. Keep paper pieces off the floor to avoid slips.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Mwangi opens by returning to the balloon: Otieno's balloon sticking to the wall, Wanjiru's rising hair, Amina's coastal home where it never works in the rainy season, and Kipchoge's question about whether the shock is like lightning. Learners first predict how engineers could use or control the same ideas in Kericho, Kisumu, Nairobi depots and Athi River. They then observe four application cases (lightning conductor, fuel tanker earthing, photocopier, electrostatic precipitator) using diagrams and a quick balloon-and-paper demonstration, and explain each with ideas from earlier lessons. In the second period learners complete the Driving Question Board, compare their Lesson 1 model with the final model, and individually write the Final Explanation answering: Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects? The lesson closes with a summary table of what was observed, learned and explained.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in groups of four and look at four images on the board: a lightning conductor on a building in Kericho tea country, a fuel tanker with a chain trailing at a Nairobi petrol depot, a school-office photocopier, and a tall chimney at a cement factory in Athi River. Mr Mwangi also holds up the rubbed balloon sticking to the wall from Lesson 1. Individually, learners write a prediction in their notebooks: (a) What do you think each device does with electric charges? (b) Which idea from our lessons might it use? Then they share with their group and agree one prediction per device, marking each as 'attract', 'earthing', 'point discharge' or 'not sure'. Kipchoge's question is posted: 'Is the shock from a jersey like lightning?' Learners predict yes or no and give a reason.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last week we learned how to detect and measure charge. Today we ask: where do these ideas matter in Kenya? Look at the four pictures. Write what you think is happening to the charges.' Give silent individual writing time, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Kipchoge asked if the shock from a jersey is like lightning. What do you predict?' Cold-call 4 learners, one per device, to give a group prediction, and 2 more for Kipchoge's question. Say: 'I am not looking for the right answer yet. I want your reasoning.' Record predictions on the board under the heading 'Predictions Before Applications'. Do not confirm or correct. Ask: 'Which of Lessons 1 to 8 will help us decide?' and list learners' answers.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction stage) with a Think-Pair-Share routine: committing to a prediction exposes the ideas learners already hold from Lessons 1 to 8 and creates a reason to examine the application evidence. Linking the images to the balloon shows that the same ideas are being transferred to technology.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: learners using the terms 'electrons', 'earthing', 'attract' or 'sharp point' in predictions; learners who say charge is 'created' or that 'positive charge moves' (note for later correction through evidence); learners who link the jersey shock to lightning. Tally on a class sheet how many groups link the tanker to earthing and the lightning conductor to a sharp point. Aim: at least 6 of 10 groups give a reason, not only a guess.

framework.learnerExperience: Station-style evidence gathering in groups (about 10 minutes per station, 4 stations, rotating, with data cards). Station 1 Lightning conductor (Kericho and Kisumu): a diagram of a pointed metal rod on a building joined by thick copper strip to a buried earth plate. Learners recall the Lesson 7 pointed-conductor readings (pointed end about 45 degrees, flat end about 20 degrees) and record what this means for where charge crowds. Station 2 Fuel tanker at a Nairobi petrol depot: a diagram of a tanker with an earthing chain or bonding wire. Learners note that fuel flowing in the pipe rubs on the pipe wall and charge can build up on the tank; they list what an uncontrolled spark could do near fuel vapour. Station 3 Photocopier at a school office and Station 4 Electrostatic precipitator at Athi River: flow-chart cards show a charged drum attracting oppositely charged powder (toner), and smoke dust particles being given negative charge and attracted to positively charged plates. At Station 3 learners also do a quick dry demonstration: pass a rubbed polythene strip over small paper pieces (about 1 cm x 1 cm) on a desk and observe them jump and stick, like toner on the drum. They record what they see, then sketch the charge signs on a data card. They also revisit the balloon humidity data: about 3 minutes on a wall at 35% relative humidity in Nairobi; under 30 seconds or none at about 80% in Mombasa.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate and ask at each station: 'What is the charge doing here? Where is it going?' At Station 1 ask: 'Looking at the pointed end reading from Lesson 7, why is a pointed rod used?' At Station 2 ask: 'What does the chain give the electrons a path to do?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before accepting any answer. Prompt: 'Use the word electrons, not charge moving, and not static electricity as an explanation.' Cold-call 2 learners at each station for a one-sentence observation before rotating. At Station 3 say: 'Keep the strip dry. What do the paper pieces do and why do some fall off again?' Prompt with Lesson 5 contact idea if needed. At Station 4 ask: 'Which charges attract: like or unlike? How do you know from Lesson 2?' Watch time and keep groups on schedule. Make sure all data cards are completed before the Explain Phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gallery-walk station analysis with data cards (Obtaining, evaluating and communicating information): moving through four contexts lets learners see the same small set of ideas (unlike charges attract, electrons transfer, point discharge, earthing) recur in different technologies, which builds transfer and consolidates the model rather than adding new facts.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check data cards for: Station 1 - charge crowds at the point, strong field, charge leaks away through the air, electrons flow through the copper strip to earth; Station 2 - chain lets electrons flow to ground, so no charge builds up and no spark; Station 3 - toner and drum have opposite signs so attract; Station 4 - dust given a charge, attracted to plates of opposite sign. Observable indicator: learners correctly use 'electrons' in at least 3 of 4 cards. Note groups who say 'static electricity' as the explanation and prompt them to name the transfer.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their groups and write a short claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) explanation for each application, then compare with their Predict Phase table. Lightning conductor: claim - it protects a building; evidence - pointed end gave a larger leaf reading (about 45 degrees) than the flat end (about 20 degrees); reasoning - charge crowds at points, the strong field ionises the air, charge leaks away gradually, and the thick copper strip and earth plate let electrons flow safely to or from the ground, which is why lightning conductors are used on buildings in Kericho and Kisumu. Fuel tanker: claim - the chain prevents sparks; reasoning - earthing lets electrons flow to the ground so charge from friction cannot build up (Lesson 6 earthing). Photocopier and precipitator: unlike charges attract. Then each group answers Kipchoge's question: how is the shock from a woollen jersey in Nairobi like and unlike lightning? Learners then do a whole-class share-out. Finally they begin the Final Explanation skeleton in pairs: they list the steps of the balloon story in order (friction, transfer of electrons, balloon negative and hair positive, hair repels itself and is attracted to the balloon, induction in wall and paper, humidity and slow leakage, 1 nC about 6 x 10^9 electrons out of about 10^23 atoms, conservation of charge).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Choose one application. Make a claim, give evidence from our lessons, and give reasoning using electrons.' Give a sentence frame on the board: 'I think ___ because the data show ___ which means electrons ___.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 5 learners to share, then ask 3 others: 'Do you agree or disagree with Wanjiru's group? What evidence supports that?' For Kipchoge's question say: 'Both are discharge of built-up charge. What is very different about the amount of charge?' Guide: the jersey shock involves a tiny charge (like the balloon's about 1 nC) while lightning involves vastly more. Correct misconceptions: 'Charges are not created, they are transferred.' and 'Positive charge does not move in a solid, electrons do.' Then say: 'Now, using the balloon, tell me the story from first rubbing to the wall.' Use a cold-call chain of 6 learners, each adding one step, while you write the steps on the board. Challenge: 'Amina, why did the balloon fail at your coastal home?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then connect to humidity: at about 80% relative humidity the balloon sticks under 30 seconds or not at all because water vapour lets the charge escape.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with a sequencing chain: CER forces learners to link evidence from earlier lessons to a mechanism, while the cold-call story chain builds the complete causal sequence of the balloon phenomenon collaboratively. Comparing the jersey shock and lightning lets learners use the same mechanism at different scales, deepening understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: a learner states that the lightning conductor works by point discharge and earthing, not by 'attracting lightning'; a learner states that the earthing chain lets electrons flow to ground; a learner uses 'transfer of electrons' and 'conserved' in the story chain; a learner explains the wall and paper attraction as induction (near side opposite charge, attraction stronger than repulsion). Count: aim for at least 80% of learners to contribute a correct step in the chain. Note common errors (for example, saying the balloon 'makes' charge or that neutral objects are repelled) and record them for the final check.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners gather at the Driving Question Board that has been built since Lesson 1. In groups they take the sticky notes of questions and sort them into 'answered with evidence', 'partly answered' and 'still unanswered'. For each answered question they write a short answer card with the lesson number and evidence (for example: 'Where do charges come from? Electrons transfer from hair to balloon in friction, L3, balloon gains about 1 nC, about 6 x 10^9 electrons'). They match the seven KICD inquiry questions to lessons: charges (L2), conductors and insulators (L4), charging conductors (L5 and L6), where charge goes (L7), detecting and measuring (L8), uses (L9). Each learner adds one new question of their own that goes beyond the unit (for example, how is the charge in a thundercloud separated?) onto a 'Next questions' area. The class reads the main driving question aloud and decides together that it has been answered.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our DQB has grown since Lesson 1. Which questions can we now answer with evidence?' Hand each group a bundle of notes and WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before they start sorting. Ask: 'What evidence shows this is answered, not just guessed?' Cold-call 5 groups to read one answer card, each from a different lesson. Say: 'Which ones are only partly answered? What would we need to find out?' Accept honest unknowns, for example, why exactly the electrons move from hair to latex (latex holds them more strongly). Ask: 'What new question do you have now?' and collect at least 8 on the board. Praise the quality of questions: 'That is a scientist's question.' Photograph or note the final DQB for the class record.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (DQB) review and sort: revisiting student-generated questions shows learners their own growth in understanding and makes the link between each lesson and the anchoring phenomenon visible. Sorting by level of evidence builds the habit of grounding claims in data, and the 'next questions' area models how science generates new inquiry.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: groups correctly place at least 5 of the 7 KICD questions with a lesson and a piece of evidence; the answer cards use the conventions (electrons, transfer, earthing, discharge); at least 8 new, relevant questions are produced; learners can state which questions remain open and why. Check for a learner who still files a question under 'answered' without evidence and ask a probing question.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out the model they drew in Lesson 1 (their initial ideas of the balloon, hair, wall and paper) and the revised versions from earlier lessons. On a fresh page they draw the final labelled particle-level model showing four parts: (1) balloon and hair before rubbing: neutral, with equal positive and negative charges; (2) after rubbing: electrons transferred from hair to latex, balloon negative (excess electrons, about 6 x 10^9 extra, around 1 nC), hair positive (deficit of electrons); (3) hair strands both positive repel each other and rise, and are attracted to the negative balloon; (4) wall and paper neutral, electrons shift slightly away from the near side, leaving the near surface positive, so attraction is stronger than repulsion; plus a note on humidity: at about 35% relative humidity charge leaks away slowly, at about 80% water vapour lets it escape. They add a small inset for one application of their choice (lightning conductor with point discharge and earthing, or tanker earthing). Then each learner writes the Final Explanation individually (8 to 10 sentences) answering: 'Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects?', using at least six key terms: friction, electrons, transfer, negative, positive, induction, repel, attract, earthing, humidity, conserved. Finally learners place their Lesson 1 model and the final model side by side and write three changes in a 'What changed in my thinking' box.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Place your Lesson 1 model next to a blank page. Now draw what is really happening, at the level of electrons. Only electrons move in solids.' Provide a checklist on the board: labels for balloon, hair, wall, paper; signs on each; arrows showing electron transfer and electron shift; note on humidity; number about 6 x 10^9 electrons of about 10^23 atoms. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before circulating. Ask: 'Why is the hair positive if it lost electrons? Why does the hair rise?' 'Why is the neutral paper attracted but not repelled?' Cold-call 3 learners to explain a part of their model to the class, and ask 2 others to critique: 'What would you add or change?' Remind them of the conventions: 'Charge is not created, it is transferred; total charge is conserved.' Walk around and check 8 to 10 learners' written explanations; give feedback with one star (strength) and one step (improvement). Close by asking 4 learners to read a key sentence of their Final Explanation, and ask the class to listen for the electron story. Invite Wanjiru, Otieno, Amina and Kipchoge's questions to be answered by name: 'Does your explanation answer Amina's coastal question? Kipchoge's lightning question?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision and model comparison (Developing and using models): placing the Lesson 1 model beside the final particle-level model makes conceptual change visible and gives learners ownership of their progress. Writing a Final Explanation with required key terms integrates all eight lessons into one causal account, consolidating the idea that the balloon phenomenon is explained by electron transfer, induction and leakage.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a four-point checklist for the Final Explanation and model: (1) friction transfers electrons from hair to latex (balloon negative, hair positive); (2) hair repulsion and attraction to balloon explained by like and unlike charges; (3) neutral wall and paper attracted by induction (near side opposite, attraction stronger than repulsion); (4) humidity and conservation of charge (including 1 nC about 6 x 10^9 electrons, tiny fraction of about 10^23 atoms). Success: at least 3 of 4 points for most learners. Observable error indicators: 'charge was created', 'positive charge moved', 'static electricity' as the explanation, or 'neutral paper is repelled'. Record scores and plan follow-up for those with fewer than 3 points. The three-change reflection should identify at least one specific shift (for example, from 'magic' or 'magnetism' to electron transfer).

FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: Driving Question: Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects? Write your own Final Explanation of the mysterious balloon. Use evidence from your lessons: the balloon-and-hair data (20 strokes, hair rising about 5 cm, balloon sticking to the wall for about 3 minutes, paper pieces jumping at about 2 cm), the rods and strips, the triboelectric order, the conduction test, the electroscope readings, and the humidity data from Nairobi and Mombasa. Answer each section in full sentences. Use the words electric charge, electron transfer, electrostatic force, conductor, insulator, induction and earthing correctly. Draw labelled particle-level diagrams where asked. Say which lesson or observation each piece of evidence comes from. Remember that only electrons move in solids.

sections.title: Part 1: Where do electric charges come from?
sections.prompt: Describe the balloon-and-hair phenomenon in Lesson 1 in your own words. Then explain where the electric charges on the balloon and hair come from. In your answer: (a) describe what atoms contain and why a normal atom is neutral, using the charge values you met; (b) explain what happens to electrons and protons when the balloon is rubbed on dry hair; (c) use the triboelectric order to say why the balloon becomes negative and the hair positive; (d) explain why we say charge is conserved and not created, using the number of electrons moved and the number of atoms in a balloon.
sections.exemplar:
In Lesson 1, a latex balloon rubbed on dry hair for 20 strokes made the hair rise and follow it up to about 5 cm. The balloon then stuck to the wall for about 3 minutes, and 1 cm x 1 cm paper pieces jumped up to it from about 2 cm away. Two rubbed balloons on threads pushed apart, and an unrubbed balloon did nothing.
(a) Atoms have positive protons (+1.6 x 10^-19 C) and neutral neutrons (0 C) in the nucleus, with negative electrons (-1.6 x 10^-19 C) around it. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so its total charge is 0 C.
(b) Friction transfers electrons from one material to the other. Electrons move from the hair to the balloon. Protons stay in the nucleus and do not move.
(c) In the triboelectric order (dry human hair (+), glass, perspex, wool/fur, silk, polythene, ebonite, latex balloon (-)), hair is higher than latex, so latex holds electrons more strongly. The balloon gains extra electrons and becomes negative. The hair has a deficit of electrons and becomes positive.
(d) The balloon gains about 1 nC (10^-9 C), which is about 6 x 10^9 electrons. The hair loses the same number. The balloon has about 10^23 atoms, so only a tiny fraction of electrons moves. Total charge stays the same, so charge is transferred, not created.

sections.title: Part 2: Why does the balloon attract or repel? Hair, balloon and the rule of forces
sections.prompt: Explain why (a) the two rubbed balloons on threads pushed apart, and (b) the hair strands rise and are pulled toward the balloon. Use the results from the rods and strips (polythene strip and perspex rod) as evidence for the rule you use. Then explain why the balloon keeps its charge for about 3 minutes on a dry day rather than losing it at once, using what you found in the conduction test with the 3 V cell and bulb. Name the type of force involved.
sections.exemplar:
The rods and strips gave the evidence for the rule. Two polythene strips rubbed with wool/fur repel, two perspex rods rubbed with silk repel, and a polythene strip and a perspex rod attract. So like charges repel and unlike charges attract. This is the electrostatic force.
(a) Each rubbed balloon gained extra electrons from the hair, so both are negative. Like charges repel, so they push apart.
(b) The hair strands lost electrons, so every strand is positive. Like charges repel, so the strands push away from each other and rise. The positive hair and the negative balloon have unlike charges, so they attract and the hair follows the balloon up to about 5 cm.
In the conduction test, the bulb lit with copper wire, aluminium foil, a steel spoon and graphite, which are conductors with free (delocalised) electrons. It did not light with a plastic ruler, dry wood, rubber, a glass rod or dry cotton cloth, which are insulators with tightly bound electrons. Latex is an insulator, so the extra electrons cannot move away. The balloon stays charged and sticks for about 3 minutes. A metal spoon is a conductor, so its charge would spread away and not stay.

sections.title: Part 3: Why do neutral paper and the wall get attracted? Contact, induction and earthing
sections.prompt: The paper pieces and the wall are neutral, yet the balloon attracts them. (a) Using a particle-level diagram and words, explain why neutral paper and wall are attracted but never repelled. (b) Explain why some paper pieces fall off after touching the balloon, using what you saw with the electroscope and the polythene strip touching the cap. (c) Compare charging by contact with charging by induction with earthing: which sign does each give, and what does earthing do? Use the electroscope observations as evidence.
sections.exemplar:
(a) The negative balloon repels electrons in the neutral paper and wall, so electrons shift slightly away. The near surface becomes positive and the far side negative, and this is induction. Diagram: balloon (-) on the left, then the wall or paper with + on the near side and - on the far side. The nearer positive charge is attracted more strongly than the farther negative charge is repelled. So there is a net attraction, and a neutral object is attracted but never repelled. This is why the paper jumps and the balloon sticks to the wall.
(b) When a negative polythene strip touched the cap of a neutral electroscope, the leaf stayed at about 30 degrees after the strip was removed. Free electrons passed from the strip to the cap, stem and leaf, so they became negative, the same sign as the strip, and repelled each other. In the same way, a paper piece that touches the negative balloon gains electrons, becomes negative and is repelled, so it falls off. Touching the cap with a finger returned the leaf to 0 degrees.
(c) Contact gives the SAME sign as the charged object, because electrons are transferred by touching. Induction with earthing gives the OPPOSITE sign. With the strip near but not touching, the leaf rose to about 30 degrees. Touching the cap with a finger (earthing) let electrons flow to the Earth, and the leaf fell to 0 degrees. After the finger and then the strip were removed, the leaf rose to about 30 degrees and stayed, showing a charge of opposite sign to the strip. In all cases only electrons move and charge is transferred, not created.

sections.title: Part 4: Charge on conductors, sparks, humidity and detecting charge
sections.prompt: (a) Using the proof-plane and electroscope readings (hollow metal can; pear-shaped conductor), explain where charge sits on a conductor. Then explain how this accounts for the small shock felt on a dry Nairobi day (for example, Wanjiru's shock after combing her hair) and for lightning conductors in Kericho and Kisumu. (b) Explain why Amina's balloon hardly works in Mombasa but works well in dry Nairobi, using the humidity figures. (c) Explain how a gold-leaf electroscope shows that the balloon is charged, how you can tell the sign of a charge, and what a bigger leaf angle tells you.
sections.exemplar:
(a) On the hollow can, the proof plane on the outside gave about 40 degrees and on the inside 0 degrees. On the pear-shaped conductor the pointed end gave about 45 degrees and the flat end about 20 degrees. Free electrons on a conductor repel each other, so they move to the outer surface and crowd at points. At a point the strong field ionises the air and charge leaks away. This is point discharge. The jersey shock is a small spark when built-up charge discharges, and a faint crackle can be heard in the dark. A lightning conductor is a pointed metal rod on top of the building, joined by thick copper strip to a buried earth plate. It lets charge leak away at the point and lets electrons flow safely to the ground, protecting buildings in Kericho and Kisumu.
(b) At about 35% humidity in dry Nairobi the balloon sticks for about 3 minutes. At about 80% humidity in Mombasa it sticks for under 30 seconds or not at all. On humid days water vapour in the air lets the balloon's charge escape, so the balloon loses its charge quickly and the effect is weak.
(c) A neutral electroscope has its leaf at 0 degrees. A charged object gives the cap, stem and leaf the same sign, so the leaf and stem repel and the leaf diverges. A rubbed balloon making the leaf rise shows that it is charged. With the electroscope negatively charged (about 30 degrees), a negative object raises the leaf above 30 degrees and a positive object lowers it below 30 degrees, so the sign can be found. A bigger angle shows more charge: 40 strokes gave about 50 degrees and 20 strokes gave about 30 degrees, because more electrons are transferred. Earthing with a finger returns the leaf to 0 degrees.

sections.title: Part 5: Applications and your complete Final Explanation
sections.prompt: (a) Choose TWO applications from lightning conductors in Kericho and Kisumu, fuel tanker earthing at Nairobi petrol depots, photocopiers, and electrostatic precipitators at Athi River cement factories. For each one, explain which electrostatics idea from the unit it uses. (b) Now write a short, connected answer to the Driving Question: Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects? Include hair, the wall, paper, humidity, and how your thinking changed from your Lesson 1 model.
sections.exemplar:
(a) Fuel tanker: a tanker trails an earthing chain. Moving fuel rubs against the tank and charge builds up by friction. Earthing lets electrons flow to the ground, so the charge cannot build up and cause a spark near fuel. Electrostatic precipitator: smoke particles are given a charge and are attracted to plates of the opposite charge. This is the rule that unlike charges attract. The particles are collected and not released into the air near Athi River. (Lightning conductor: point discharge and earthing. Photocopier: attraction between unlike charges.)
(b) Electric charges are not created. They come from electrons that already exist in atoms. A neutral atom has equal protons and electrons. When I rub the balloon on dry hair, electrons transfer from the hair to the latex because latex holds electrons more strongly. The balloon gains about 1 nC, about 6 x 10^9 electrons, out of about 10^23 atoms. The balloon becomes negative and the hair positive, and the total charge is conserved. The hair strands, all positive, repel each other and rise, and the unlike charges of the hair and balloon attract. Two rubbed balloons are both negative, so they repel. The negative balloon induces charge separation in the neutral wall and paper, with the near side positive. The attraction is stronger than the repulsion, so the paper jumps and the balloon sticks, and a neutral object is never repelled. Paper pieces that touch the balloon gain electrons, become negative and fall off. Latex is an insulator, so the balloon keeps its charge for about 3 minutes on a dry day. On humid days, such as in Mombasa at about 80%, water vapour lets the charge escape, so the effect is weak. In Lesson 1 my model only described what I saw. My final model shows electron transfer, charge separation and charge leaking away.

rubric.criterion: Origin of charge (electron transfer and conservation)
rubric.excellent: Clearly explains that charges come from electrons already in atoms, that electrons move from hair to latex and protons stay put, uses the triboelectric order and the 1 nC, 6 x 10^9 electrons, 10^23 atoms figures, and states that charge is transferred, not created.
rubric.proficient: Explains that electrons transfer from hair to balloon so the balloon is negative and hair positive, and mentions that charge is conserved, but gives few or no numbers or no reason from the triboelectric order.
rubric.developing: Says that rubbing creates charge or does not say what moves, or mixes up which object is positive and which is negative.

rubric.criterion: Attraction and repulsion, including neutral objects
rubric.excellent: Uses like-repel and unlike-attract with evidence from the rods and strips, and explains attraction of neutral paper and wall by induction (charge separation, nearer charge attracts more), with a labelled particle diagram and the point that neutral objects are never repelled.
rubric.proficient: Applies the rule to balloons and hair and mentions that neutral objects are attracted because of charge separation, but with limited detail or no diagram.
rubric.developing: Only describes attraction and repulsion without giving a cause, or says that neutral objects are repelled or that positive charge moves.

rubric.criterion: Conductors, insulators, charging methods and distribution
rubric.excellent: Correctly links free versus tightly bound electrons to the conduction test and to the balloon keeping its charge, and compares contact (same sign) with induction and earthing (opposite sign). Explains charge on outer surfaces and at points with point discharge, using the electroscope and proof-plane readings.
rubric.proficient: Correctly states the difference between conductors and insulators and between contact and induction, and gives some of the readings, with some gaps in explaining distribution or earthing.
rubric.developing: Confuses conductors with insulators or contact with induction, or gives no use of the readings.

rubric.excellent: Explains the electroscope (same sign on leaf and stem, bigger angle means more charge, sign test, earthing), explains humidity using 35% and 80% and the 3 minutes against under 30 seconds figures, and links two applications to the correct idea.
rubric.proficient: Explains how the electroscope detects charge and mentions humidity and one application correctly, with few data values.

rubric.criterion: Use of evidence, vocabulary and coherence
rubric.excellent: Uses exact data and lesson evidence, uses terms such as electric charge, electrostatic force, discharge, earthing and induction accurately, and gives a connected final answer that shows how the Lesson 1 model has changed.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: Where do electric charges come from? Why does a rubbed balloon attract or repel other objects?

lessons.title: The Mysterious Balloon: What Invisible Force Is at Work?
lessons.observed: After 20 strokes on dry hair, the rubbed balloon made hair strands rise and follow it up to about 5 cm, stuck to the wall for about 3 minutes, and made 1 cm x 1 cm paper pieces jump up when held about 2 cm above them, with some falling off again. Two rubbed balloons on threads pushed apart. An unrubbed balloon did nothing. The effect is weak or absent on humid days (Mombasa, about 80%) and strong on dry days (Nairobi, about 35%).
lessons.learned: Rubbing makes the balloon able to pull on hair, wall and paper without touching them, and to push away another rubbed balloon. The effect is not the same as a magnet, it fades with time and it depends on the weather. We now have many questions on our DQB.
lessons.explained: So far we can only describe what happens: something invisible passes between the rubbed balloon and other objects, and rubbing and dry air seem to matter. Our initial models are hunches, and we do not yet know where the effect comes from or why the balloon sometimes attracts and sometimes repels.

lessons.title: What Are Electric Charges? Atoms, Protons, Electrons and the Rule of Attraction and Repulsion
lessons.observed: Two polythene strips rubbed with wool/fur repel; two perspex rods rubbed with silk repel; a polythene strip and a perspex rod attract; unrubbed strips and rods do nothing. Proton charge is +1.6 x 10^-19 C, electron charge is -1.6 x 10^-19 C and neutron charge is 0 C.
lessons.learned: Atoms contain positive protons and neutral neutrons in the nucleus with negative electrons around it. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so the total charge is 0 C. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract through the electrostatic force.
lessons.explained: The two rubbed balloons in Lesson 1 pushed apart because they carry the same type of charge, while the balloon and hair attracted because they carry opposite types. We still need to find out how rubbing gives objects their charge and why neutral objects such as paper and the wall are also attracted.

lessons.title: Charging by Friction: Who Wins the Electrons?
lessons.observed: We rubbed pairs of materials (glass with silk, ebonite with fur, perspex with wool/fur, polythene with silk, balloon with hair) and tested them against a negative polythene strip and a positive perspex rod. Rod and cloth had opposite signs, shown by repulsion. The balloon was negative and the hair positive. Unrubbed objects showed no effect.
lessons.learned: Friction transfers electrons from one material to the other. Protons stay in the nucleus. The sign depends on the material pair, following the triboelectric order: dry human hair (+), glass, perspex, wool/fur, silk, polythene, ebonite, latex balloon (-). Charge is conserved: the balloon gains about 1 nC (6 x 10^9 electrons) and the hair loses the same amount, out of about 10^23 atoms.
lessons.explained: When I rub the balloon on my hair, electrons transfer from the hair to the balloon because latex holds electrons more strongly. The balloon becomes negative and the hair positive. The hair strands, all positive, repel each other and rise, and they are attracted to the negative balloon. Charge is not created. Still to explain: why the balloon sticks to the neutral wall and attracts paper, and why humidity makes it fail.

lessons.title: Conductors and Insulators: Why Does the Balloon Keep Its Charge While a Metal Spoon Does Not?
lessons.observed: The bulb lit with copper wire, aluminium foil, a steel spoon and graphite. It did not light with a plastic ruler, dry wood, rubber, a glass rod or dry cotton cloth in the 3 V circuit.
lessons.learned: Conductors have free (delocalised) electrons that can move through the material; insulators have tightly bound electrons. Only electrons move in solids. The latex balloon is an insulator, so the electrons it gains from the hair stay on it.
lessons.explained: The balloon is negative and holds its extra electrons (about 6 x 10^9 for 1 nC) because latex is an insulator, so the charge cannot move away and the balloon stays charged and sticks for about 3 minutes on a dry day.

lessons.title: Charging by Contact: Why Do Paper Pieces Touch the Balloon and Then Fall Off?
lessons.observed: The leaf of a neutral electroscope stayed at about 30 degrees after a negative polythene strip touched the cap and was removed (0 degrees before; about 30 degrees also when the strip was only near). Touching the cap with a finger returned the leaf to 0 degrees. Paper pieces jumped up to the rubbed balloon and some fell off again after touching it.
lessons.learned: A conductor touched by a charged object gains the SAME sign of charge by transfer of electrons. Free electrons in the conductor let the charge spread to the leaf, and like charges repel, so the leaf stays raised. Charge is transferred, not created.
lessons.explained: The negative strip passed extra electrons to the cap, stem and leaf, so they all became negative and repelled each other. In the same way, a paper piece that touches the negative balloon gains electrons, becomes negative, and is repelled, so it falls off. This adds one more step to the balloon-and-hair explanation, though why neutral paper is attracted at first is still to be explained.

lessons.title: Charging by Induction and Earthing: Charging Without Touching
lessons.observed: A neutral electroscope with a negative polythene strip brought near the cap, not touching: the leaf rose to about 30 degrees and fell back to 0 degrees when the strip was removed. With the strip near and a finger touching the cap (earthing), the leaf fell to 0 degrees. After removing the finger and then the strip, the leaf rose to about 30 degrees and stayed up. Neutral paper pieces jumped to the negative balloon and the balloon stuck to the wall, with no repulsion seen.
lessons.learned: A charged object can separate charge in a neutral object without touching it (induction). Earthing lets electrons flow to or from the Earth, and charging by induction with earthing gives the OPPOSITE sign, while contact gives the SAME sign. Only electrons move, and charge is not created but transferred.
lessons.explained: The negative balloon repels electrons in the neutral paper and wall, leaving the near surface positive and the far side negative. The nearer positive charge is attracted more strongly than the farther negative charge is repelled, so a neutral object is attracted but never repelled. This explains why the paper jumps and the balloon sticks to the wall. On humid days, such as in Mombasa, the balloon's charge leaks away, so the effect is weak or short-lived.

lessons.title: Distribution of Charge on Conductors: Outer Surfaces, Points, Sparks and Lightning Conductors
lessons.observed: We observed that a charged hollow metal can gave an electroscope leaf reading of about 40 degrees when the proof plane touched the outside and 0 degrees when it touched the inside. On the pear-shaped conductor, the pointed end gave about 45 degrees and the flat end about 20 degrees.
lessons.learned: We learned that the free electrons on a charged conductor repel each other and move to the outer surface, and that charge is most concentrated at points. At a point, the strong field ionises the air and charge leaks away (point discharge), while earthing lets charge flow safely to the ground.
lessons.explained: This explains why a woollen jersey shock in dry Nairobi is a small spark (a discharge) and why lightning conductors, with a pointed rod joined by thick copper strip to a buried earth plate, protect buildings in Kericho and Kisumu. It also adds to our model of how electrons, not created charge, move and build up around the balloon, hair, wall and paper.

lessons.title: Detecting and Measuring Charge: The Gold-Leaf Electroscope
lessons.observed: Record what you observed with the gold-leaf electroscope: the leaf at 0 degrees when neutral; about 30 degrees with a negative polythene strip (20 strokes); the leaf staying up after contact; about 50 degrees with 40 strokes; the angle going above 30 degrees with a negative object and below 30 degrees with a positive object; and 0 degrees after earthing with a finger.
lessons.learned: Write what you learned: a gold-leaf electroscope detects charge because the leaf and stem carry the same sign and repel; a bigger leaf divergence shows more charge; an increase on a charged electroscope shows the same sign and a decrease shows the opposite sign; earthing lets electrons flow to or from the Earth and discharges the electroscope.
lessons.explained: Explain how this helps answer the Driving Question: the rubbed balloon is shown to be charged because it makes the leaf diverge, its negative sign can be tested, and the amount of charge relates to the number of strokes because more electrons are transferred, not created.
